item.title: Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries
item.description:
Key Points Introduction Over the past two months, we have been tracking a campaign that abuses the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude to spread a custom malware chain we call Yoba. The attackers use fake GitHub projects that pretend to be AI desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude […]

The post Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
Key Points

  • Check Point Research discovered a campaign we track as Yoba where attackers abuse the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, creating fake GitHub projects that pretend to be desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus.
  • The malware is placed next to legitimate, signed executables from OpenAI and Anthropic so it can be loaded indirectly, a technique commonly known as DLL sideloading, which is often used to bypass security protections.
  • This campaign demonstrates strong operational security (OPSEC) by avoiding dedicated command-and-control (C2) infrastructure and instead relying on Telegram, Tor, Catbox, and DNS over HTTPS (DoH).
  • The actor behind the campaign shows indicators that suggest Russian origins and appears to operate primarily in the UTC-4 time zone.


Introduction

Over the past two months, we have been tracking a campaign that abuses the popularity of AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude to spread a custom malware chain we call Yoba. The attackers use fake GitHub projects that pretend to be AI desktop applications like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. These projects look convincing and use real GitHub infrastructure, which helps them appear legitimate to potential victims. The website exhibits search-targeted content and suspicious installer-delivery tactics consistent with an SEO-poisoning lure.

Inside the installers, there is a malicious component we refer to as the YobaDropper. This dropper includes another component, the YobaLoader, which is responsible for contacting attacker-controlled infrastructure and fetching the final payload. In this report, we describe how victims are lured to these fake projects, how the YobaDropper and YobaLoader work together, and how the attackers ultimately use this chain to run unwanted software on infected systems.


GitHub Repositories

The initial access occurred via malicious GitHub repositories. The projects were impersonating ChatGPT and Claude related models, more specifically GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and Claude Opus. No manipulation of fake engagement (stars/forks) was in place.

Aside from the repositories, GitHub.io pages were used to describe the capabilities of the software, while the malware was hosted as a release.

These phishing landing pages contain download links that point directly to the malicious ZIP releases hosted on GitHub.

While the repositories do not show signs of fake engagement (such as artificially inflated stars or forks) that would promote them within GitHub’s own search, they still appear among the top results on Google. This is most likely due to SEO poisoning, where the attackers optimize titles, descriptions, and hosting domains to make their malicious projects rank highly in external search engines.

Each repository uses a different email address (edwardcarlsonmkym[@]outlook[.]com, daxschneiderdjuu[@]outlook[.]com, and rioprestonlfyx[@]outlook[.]com), and the uploader appears to operate in UTC+4, UTC-4, and UTC+3 respectively. This inconsistency likely reflects a deliberate attempt to obscure the threat actor’s true operational timezone.

Repositories’ initial commits:

Repository: /gpt-5-6/sol-free-desktop
==================================================
[2026-07-16T14:39:40Z] Author: gpt-5-6	
tree aebceccb0f3303806c35a73da865b684594487c1
author gpt-5-6 <edwardcarlsonmkym@outlook.com> 1784212780 +0400
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1784212780 +0400

Initial commit
==================================================

Repository: /gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io
==================================================
[2026-07-16T14:44:31Z] Author: gpt-5-6	
tree 249dae41d64583a6a9ebcb60e3ad36d6216dd6e4
author gpt-5-6 <edwardcarlsonmkym@outlook.com> 1784213071 +0400
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1784213071 +0400

Initial commit
==================================================

Repository: /opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github.io
==================================================
[2026-08-31T21:33:26Z] Author: opus-5-0	
tree 46ae1f147cf70d4df1471f0e9df46b654d11fe9c
author opus-5-0 <rioprestonlfyx@outlook.com> 1788212006 -0400
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1788212006 -0400

Create readme.md
==================================================

Repository: /gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io
==================================================
[2026-09-04T22:56:13Z] Author: gpt-6-astra	
tree 028bfd4c1041dc1f030c9480a463366e6089e661
author gpt-6-astra <daxschneiderdjuu@outlook.com> 1788562573 +0300
committer GitHub <noreply@github.com> 1788562573 +0300

Initial commit
==================================================

Although the first repository was created around July 2026, the first two malicious releases were not uploaded until the end of August, and a third malicious release followed approximately five days later.

Release: /gpt-5-6/gpt-5-6.github.io/releases/tag/v5.6.0
[2026-08-30T19:15:44Z] gpt-5-6 Uploaded sol-setup.zip (application/zip) (269)
==================================================

Release: /opus-5-0/opus-5-0.github.io/releases/tag/Release_v5.0.0
[2026-08-31T21:38:13Z] opus-5-0 uploaded Setup-Claude.zip (application/zip) (82)
==================================================

Release: /gpt-6-astra/gpt-6-astra.github.io/releases/tag/Astra
[2026-09-04T23:14:11Z] gpt-6-astra Uploaded GPT-6-Astra-Setup.zip (application/zip) (352)

Malicious zip files hosted on GitHub and other legitimate platforms are usually password-protected, since this prevents automated tools from unpacking and therefore analyzing them. However, neither of these repositories used password protection, as the binaries already had very low detection rates thanks to their anti-sandbox and other anti-analysis techniques.

While the two ChatGPT-related releases and their repositories were created about five days apart, the ZIP files contain mostly the same files, including the malicious components, and they maintain the same IoCs.

By adding the compilation timestamps to this these time-related operations, we are able to determine which files appear to contain the malicious functionality without performing any initial analysis.

The file that immediately stands out is winmm.dll, which was compiled the same day it was added to the ZIP archive. This suggests it is the component with the malicious functionality, while the other files serve to make the package appear legitimate. The compilation timestamp also indicates the actor is operating in the UTC-4 timezone.

Furthermore, Setup.exe, a legitimate signed OpenAI executable, is used during execution to sideload the malicious DLL. The Setup-Claude.zip file contains the same structure, though in this case Setup.exe is a legitimate signed Claude executable.


YobaDropper – winmm.dll

The malicious DLL contains multiple export names, suggesting that the legitimate winmm.dll has been spoofed. As in many other cases, these exports exist but their code has been stripped out, leaving them mostly empty and reducing the size of the binary.

All 180 exports contain just a return instruction (C3) followed by NOPs (90), and DllEntryPoint is the only one containing actual code.


Anti-Analysis, Pre-Checks

The first function implements an anti-sandbox technique: the malware hashes the basename of its host executable and checks whether the checksum matches the hardcoded value 0xE6C2F326. The hashing algorithm has been identified as DJB2, which other malware families have also used in the past. The malware expects to run under the name Setup.exe, so this check fails if the DLL is executed on its own inside a sandbox environment.

Although a failed check does not terminate the process, the DLL performs 200,000 iterations of Sleep(5500), amounting to approximately 12.73 days, while repeatedly appending the decoded filler string pddy to a local UTF-16 buffer.

In the second function, the malware checks whether the infected user is located in a CIS country by inspecting the system’s keyboard layout. Ukraine was historically included in such checks, but it is not in the list used by recent malware.

The language check is unusual. Instead of comparing the victim’s keyboard language ID against hardcoded values, the malware checks whether the ID falls within the range 0x19–0x44. For IDs in that range, it tests the corresponding bit in the bitmask 0xEC0400C8401 to determine whether the language belongs to a CIS-region country, with an explicit exception for ID 0x22 (Ukrainian). Bazarloader has used a similar technique in the past, with the bitmask 0xD8080190C03.

Language IDs excluded from the infection:

The malware continues to resolve Windows API functions dynamically from kernel32.dll and ntdll.dll by comparing hashes of the exported function names. The hashing algorithm is again DJB2, with the initial value 0x1505.

The last check before the malware unpacks and deploys the embedded payload tests whether the process is running with administrator privileges. If it is not, the malware displays the message “Please run this program as Administrator.” to the victim and terminates itself, requiring the user to rerun it with elevated privileges.


Deploying Phase

The dropper contains multiple XOR-encrypted strings that are decrypted when needed. These strings include the file paths where the embedded binaries are dropped, as well as the decryption keys.

It creates a directory under ProgramData named WMProcess. Then it copies the original WMPDMC.exe from System32 into this newly created folder. Next, it decrypts the embedded payload using the string IRANNUMBERONE as the XOR seed and drops the decrypted payload in the same folder under the name wmpdui.dll.

Using scheduled tasks, the dropper maintains persistence by leveraging the legitimate executable, which will sideload the malicious payload. To make the task appear legitimate, it sets the author to Microsoft Corporation and the description to Collects device metadata for Windows Media Player.. It also sets the boot-trigger delay to PT3M, which corresponds to a 3-minute delay after system startup, and configures the task to run under the Local System account (S-1-5-18).


YobaLoader – wmpdui.dll

The second-stage payload contains the same code as the dropper, which indicates that the same developer is responsible for both components.

The same anti-sandbox technique is used, forcing the malware to be run only by WMPDMC.exe. It again checks the hash of the process basename, and only continues execution if this value matches the hardcoded hash 0x552751E3.

The dropper uses the DJB2 hashing algorithm to hash and verify the process name and to resolve Windows API functions, both with the same seed 0x1505. The loader (YobaLoader) also uses DJB2 for the process name with the same seed as the dropper, but for resolving Windows API functions it uses a different seed, 0x1DEB.

The developer reused the same string-hashing algorithm but changed the seed (0x1505 in the dropper, 0x1DEB in the loader) to separate the hash spaces for each stage, complicating analysis, and reducing the effectiveness of hash-based detection and automated tooling.


Network

The downloader uses an interesting process to obtain the next-stage payload. It first decrypts multiple strings using a simple XOR operation, among these strings is the URL of a Telegram channel, t[.]me/yoba_fanclub. It then visits this channel using the user-agent string Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64;) and parses the HTML source to extract the src URL of the element with the class tgme_page_photo_image. This class refers to the location where the channel’s profile image is hosted.

It downloads the image and uses the last 50 bytes as a seed to generate a domain based on three lists of dictionary words, which are decrypted as part of the DGA algorithm. This DGA algorithm uses three sets of strings:

  1. Adjectives
  2. Nouns
  3. Verbs

Finally, it generates and appends an integer value in the range 0–999. The generated domain has the following format, "$adjective-$noun-$verb-$digit.dedyn[.]io". By changing the image of the Telegram channel, a new domain can be generated.

The following Python snippet represents the DGA algorithm:

"""
Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research
"""
from pathlib import Path
import sys

ADJECTIVES = [
    "silver", "amber", "wild", "tiny", "brave", "lucky", "calm",
    "sharp", "swift", "bright", "quiet", "bold", "gentle", "fierce",
    "royal", "mystic", "username", "degenerate", "allblack", "kizta",
    "graf",
]
NOUNS = [
    "tiger", "river", "stone", "cloud", "wolf", "ocean", "forest",
    "mountain", "eagle", "raven", "ember", "comet", "fox", "dragon",
    "piano", "viper", "yoba", "yyoba", "static", "cpp", "example",
]
VERBS = [
    "runs", "jumps", "sings", "sleeps", "flies", "hunts", "burns",
    "floats", "shines", "whispers", "roars", "dreams", "strikes",
    "glides", "watches", "hides", "duty", "free",
]

FNV_MULTIPLIER = 0x1000193
MASK64 = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF

def hash_bytes(data: bytes, seed: int) -> int:
    value = seed
    for byte in data:
        value = ((value ^ byte) * FNV_MULTIPLIER) & MASK64
    return value

def generate_domain(image_path: str) -> str:
    image = Path(image_path).read_bytes()
    if len(image) < 50:
        raise ValueError("Image must contain at least 50 bytes")

    tail = image[-50:]

    adjective = ADJECTIVES[hash_bytes(tail, 0x811C9DC5) % len(ADJECTIVES)]
    noun = NOUNS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xAF0154A5) % len(NOUNS)]
    verb = VERBS[hash_bytes(tail, 0xFE5439E4) % len(VERBS)]
    number = hash_bytes(tail, 0xFFA7471A) % 1000

    return f"{adjective}-{noun}-{verb}-{number}.dedyn[.]io"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    image_file = sys.argv[1]
    print(generate_domain(image_file))

It then queries Google’s DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) API to obtain an encrypted command from a DNS TXT record, using a URL of the form https://dns[.]google/resolve?name=$DGA&type=TXT.

By relying on a DoH service and common file-hosting platforms, the actor aims to bypass passive DNS monitoring and some gateway-based security protections, making their command-and-control traffic harder to distinguish from regular user activity.

It decodes the Base64-encoded data field from the JSON response and validates it using Ed25519 signature verification with the public key b5c2d20623d4e6647d06a42864edd8629f82c5c384b243fdaeeeca24b3873d64. Once the signature validation succeeds, it decrypts the decoded value using AES in ECB mode with the key 1d0d1368b4d53f3a6322cf40e84e63db.

Decrypted response: 1https://files.catbox[.]moe/z5zpy9.dat

The downloader retrieves the encrypted payload and decrypts it using the same AES key and ECB mode that were previously used for the DNS data.

The malware provides three methods for deploying the downloaded payload. The selected method is indicated by the first character of the decrypted response that follows the URL (1/2/3):

  1. Injects the downloaded payload into svchost.exe (NtWriteVirtualMemory/NtCreateThreadEx). It enumerates running processes and, using the hashing algorithm with the seed 0x1DEB, searches for the hash value 0xC26CDEA5, which corresponds to svchost.exe.
  2. Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.exe file and executes it. Before running the executable, the downloader removes the Zone.Identifier alternate data stream, which is hidden metadata used by Windows to track the origin of downloaded files.
  3. Saves the payload as a %TEMP%\$10_rand_char\$10_rand_char.ps1 PowerShell script and invokes it with the following parameters: -WindowStyle Hidden -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File.

Finally, the injected payload into svchost.exe is an XMRig 6.26.0 miner with a hidden command line targeting a TLS-enabled onion mining endpoint through a local Tor SOCKS5 proxy. It can unpack and start Tor 0.4.9.12 plus lyrebird 0.8.1, monitor user-input activity to pause mining, and conditionally load the WinRing0 driver service for MSR-based mining optimization.

Although we observed an XMRig cryptominer as the final payload in this campaign, the YobaLoader is a generic loader. The operator can supply any PE or PowerShell payload via the signed DNS TXT tasking, so future waves may deliver different malware families.


Past Yoba Versions

Yoba exposes, through the same hashing algorithm it uses for anti-analysis, the specific process name under which it expects to run. Even without having full visibility into the campaign from the very beginning, analysts can still infer which targeted software was used to lure users by correlating this expected process name with the fake AI applications promoted on the associated GitHub repositories and GitHub Pages sites.

Earlier YobaDropper observed in the wild appeared in early June 2026. In this campaign, the dropper was sideloaded by a process named Cursor.exe (hash: 0x56221573). It remains unclear whether Cursor.exe was a legitimate signed binary. The majority of the functionality in this early variant is consistent with the newer versions of both the dropper and the loader.

YobaDropper shows two main differences between its older and newer versions:

  1. Unpacking logic: In the oldest version, the buffer is first Base64-decoded and then XOR-decrypted to extract the YobaLoader. In the newer version, the developer removed the Base64-decoding step and performs only XOR decryption, simplifying the unpacking process.
  2. Execution method: The second change concerns how YobaLoader is triggered. The newer version uses Scheduled Tasks to start the copied legitimate host and sideload the loader, whereas the first discovered version creates the shortcut msdefender_scheduler{7940-8490-6670-1081}.lnk in the Startup folder. This shortcut executes a copied %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\msdtc.exe and sideloads %APPDATA%\Microsaft Difendir\mswsock.dll.

Earlier version of YobaLoader contains language checks and excludes only Russia from infection. In later versions, these checks were moved to the dropper stage and expanded to exclude additional CIS countries, shifting regional filtering earlier in the infection chain.

While the overall DGA logic remains the same, the early variant uses the extension .aber[.]ir instead of .dedyn[.]io. In addition, instead of injecting into svchost.exe, this variant injects into a different running process identified only by its hashed name 0x21BD94C2.

The initial loader also implements several anti-analysis techniques that have been removed from the newer versions of the malware:

1. Anti-debugging
It enumerates all kernel object types and reads their TypeName values. Each type name is hashed using DJB2 with the seed 0x1DEB until the hash matches 0xCF9EE149, which corresponds to DebugObject. If a DebugObject is found, it indicates that a debugger is or was active, and in that case the malware terminates itself.

2. Anti-VM
The malware uses a VM/sandbox-detection scoring function while running several hardware fingerprinting checks. The maximum score is 6, and the minimum required to continue the infection chain is 3. The checks include:

  • Hypervisor-present bit and CPUID timing (via RDTSCP).
  • Hypervisor vendor signature string (CPUID leaf 0x40000000).
  • CPU brand string sanity checks (CPUID leaves 0x80000002–0x80000004).
  • SMBIOS-based firmware fingerprinting (GetSystemFirmwareTable–RSMB)

Despite these small differences in early anti-analysis behavior, the Telegram channel and the profile image used as the seed for the DGA remain the same as in the newer variants, indicating that the operator retained the same infrastructure while iterating on the loader’s evasion logic.


Conclusion

The Yoba campaign shows how attackers can use trusted platforms and the current interest in AI tools to distribute malware in a way that looks believable and harmless at first glance. By packaging their code together with well-known software names and hosting it on GitHub, they lower the chances that users or basic security checks will immediately flag the files as suspicious.
Although the underlying techniques are more advanced than typical commodity malware, the main goals remain straightforward: gain a foothold on the victim’s system, avoid easy detection, and then run the attacker’s chosen payload. Organizations should be cautious about installing “AI helpers” or similar tools from unverified repositories and should enforce policies that restrict running software from unknown sources. Combining user awareness with basic technical controls.


Indicators of Compromise


Yara Rules

rule yoba_dropper
{
    meta:
        author = "@Tera0017/Check Point Research"
        description = "YobaDropper"
    strings:
        $code1 = {00 BB 40 0D 03 00 B9 7C 15 00 00 FF D6 31 C0}
        $code2 = {BA 05 15 00 00 0F BE 08 84 C9 74 0A 6B D2 21}
        $code3 = {53 B9 75 EE 40 70 48 83 EC 20}
        $code4 = {BA 5C CD 17 E5 48 89 C1 E8 73 00 00 00}
        $code5 = {0F C8 89 C0 4? 39 ?? 74 1? (49 0F AF C0| 48 69 C0 ?? ?? ?? ??) (4C 01 C8| 48 05 ?? ?? ?? ??) 49 89 C? 49 C1 E? 18 45 30 [2] 4? FF ?? EB}
    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 2 of them
}

rule yoba_loader
{
    meta:
        author = "@Tera0017/Check Point Research"
        description = "YobaLoader"
    strings:
        $code1 = {B9 80 A8 12 01 FF ?? ?? E9}
        $code2 = {BA EB 1D 00 00 0F BE 08 84 C9 74 0A 6B D2 21}
        $code3 = {B9 5B 80 EF B7 E8}
        $code4 = {BA F5 8B 2E F2 48 89 C1}
        $code5 = {B5 C2 D2 06 23 D4 E6 64 7D 06 A4 28 64 ED D8 62 9F 82 C5 C3 84 B2 43 FD AE EE CA 24 B3 87 3D 64}
        $code6 = {1D 0D 13 68 B4 D5 3F 3A 63 22 CF 40 E8 4E 63 DB}
        $code7 = {40 80 FE 32 74 42 40 80 FE 33 74 66 40 80 FE 31}
        $code8 = {41 81 F8 A5 DE 6C C2}
    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 2 of them
}

The post Tricks from the Past deployed via signed ChatGPT and Claude binaries appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
item.description: We are launching a PHP Capture the Flag challenge integrated with our Bug Bounty program to test our WAF protections. Security researchers are invited to bypass our defenses and capture the flag to help make the Internet safer.
item.content:encoded:
Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.

Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection.

As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.

Put our WAF to the test

Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.

That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.

How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works

We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag.

The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.

Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.

Challenge requirements

This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:

  1. All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF.
  2. Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.
  3. Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.
  4. Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:
    1. The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.
    2. Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.
    3. An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.
    4. The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.
    5. What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.

UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.

Awards require a materially distinct bypass method or exploit payload, even for the same PHP CVE. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.

We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s privacy notice before testing.

Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected /php/* endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.

In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.

Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.

Not a substitute for patching

Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the latest PHP security advisories and apply the relevant updates.

Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.

We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to php-rce.cloudflare.app if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

item.title: Hiding Capabilities in AI Models
item.description:
Interesting research: “AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities”

Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses...
item.content:encoded:
Interesting research: “AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities”

Abstract: Capability evaluations aim to surface dangerous model behaviors before deployment, but their reliability depends on the assumption that hidden capabilities can be elicited. We show this assumption does not hold under adversarial conditions by constructing backdoor attacks that embed encrypted neural networks within host model weights, decrypting and executing them only upon receiving a secret trigger. Using digital lockers, these hidden circuits remain provably hard to elicit and interpret under cryptographic assumptions, even given full access to model weights, extending prior work from hiding fixed strings to arbitrary computations. We implement our proof of concept constructions in PyTorch and evaluate elicitation through fine-tuning, weight noising, gradient-based trigger search, and latent adversarial training, using a small chemical reaction prediction task as a proxy for CBRN-relevant capabilities. Our results demonstrate resistance to these methods and, together with our cryptographic guarantees, reveal a limit of elicitation-based capability audits. We release our models to support the improvement of defenses.

item.title: Apple Patches for October 2026, (Mon, Oct 26th)
item.description: Apple today released patches for 304 vulnerabilties. This number is still in line with prior Apple updates, and comes just about a month after the last apple update.
item.content:encoded:
Apple today released patches for 304 vulnerabilties. This number is still in line with prior Apple updates, and comes just about a month after the last apple update.

Noteworthy Issue:

CVE-2026-86950: This is an already exploited vulnerability in CoreGraphics, and was patched originally a month ago. This month's update delivers the corresponding patches for iOS 18.

No new vulnerability is marked as already exploited.

Other Interesting issues:

CVE-2026-86990: A malicious app may access the camera without user permissions.
CVE-2026-28864: A local attacker may gain access to user's Keychain items.

item.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
item.description: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
item.content:encoded:
On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected.

Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens.

After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.

Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs.

What happened

GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day.  

This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue.

The second was a bug in how SGLang handled the resulting over-length requests in disaggregated prefill/decode mode. A prompt that did not fit the pool was internally marked as rejected and replaced with a one-token placeholder, but instead of aborting the request and returning a client error, prefill generated the KV cache for the placeholder prompt and transferred it to the decode node. The decode node received a "transfer complete" message and assumed that prefill overwrote the KV cache from previous requests with the full prompt for this request, when in fact it left the majority of the previous state intact. The decode node subsequently generated a response while attending over stale cache pages that still held data from earlier requests. As a result, responses to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens could contain data from other users' GLM 5.3 sessions.

Immediate remediation

After disabling the model, we took the following actions to correct this vulnerability before restoring public access to it:

To fix our configuration, we made the pool hold the full context. We adjusted our GLM 5.3 configuration to match our GLM 5.2 configuration, which freed enough GPU memory that the prefill KV pool now holds about 2.04 million tokens, roughly twice the 1,048,576-token context length. A prompt that fits the context window now always fits the pool, so the rejection path is never reached for a valid request. This alone prevents the bug from being exercised.

To fix the engine, we also made the rejection path safe. Relying on pool size alone is fragile: any change to quantization, tensor parallelism, CUDA graph sizes, or a future model version changes the pool size in a way that's easy to miss. Furthermore, there may be other situations in which the prefill scheduler can reject a request and trigger the same bug. To prevent this, we also patched the engine so that a request carrying a pending rejection is retired at the disaggregation admission queue, with its original error, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer happens. We proposed this upstream as #38704, which also had the decode node verify that the number of tokens transferred matches the number it reserved. The fix was already on SGLang main in #36988, merged September 6 for a related failure path but not yet released. The maintainers also merged #38935, which rejects these requests earlier, following our approach.

We validated both changes against the researcher's reproduction script and our own canary-marker tests before restoring the model.

Background: how we serve GLM 5.3

Workers AI runs GLM 5.3 with SGLang in a disaggregated configuration: a pool of prefill GPUs processes the prompt and produces the model's KV cache for it, then hands that cache over remote direct memory access (RDMA), via Mooncake, to a pool of decode GPUs that generate the response. We have written about this architecture before in our posts on high-performance LLMs and smaller, faster, safer models.

The KV cache in GPU memory is a shared pool of fixed-size pages. Each request is assigned pages when it is admitted and releases them when it finishes. Pages are not currently zeroed between requests; the next request that gets a page simply overwrites it. This approach is common among inference engines and is necessary to achieve the best performance, but it means that the inference engine is responsible for tracking ownership of these memory pages. KV cache page ownership and lifetime tracking has to deal with not just shared ownership within a node (KV cache offload and token generation both access the memory with different lifetimes), but also ownership that is technically shared with the remote prefill node (which holds a simultaneous mutable reference to the page).

Furthermore, the size of this pool is not a configuration value. SGLang sizes it at startup from whatever GPU memory remains after loading the model weights. The model's advertised context length is a separate configuration value. Nothing forces the two to agree, and it is our job to check that they do.

Issue one: misconfiguration

On our GLM 5.3 prefill nodes with our configuration, the pool came to 681,280 tokens while the model's context length is 1,048,576 tokens. The selected KV pool size is printed by SGLang in logs during startup and exposed as a metric. We were aware of this size mismatch; however, during pre-launch testing we observed successful HTTP status codes and a streaming body with no error frames during benchmarking. We assumed that the engine was capable of gracefully handling the difference between the KV cache pool and requested context window via streaming or some other mechanism.

This was one critical gap in our testing: we only validated HTTP response codes and engine performance at long contexts, without validating model output and coherence. We now check KV pool size against context length directly, from the running engine, before any disaggregated deployment change ships, rather than inferring it from response codes.

Issue two: SGLang bug

In v0.5.21, the SGLang team has now addressed this bug in how it was handling prompts longer than the KV pool size. Here’s what was happening before.

When a prompt arrived that was longer than the KV pool could hold, SGLang's scheduler rejected it. The rejection path (Req.set_finish_with_abort) recorded the error to be returned to the client and swapped the prompt for a one-token placeholder so that the request could drain through the normal batch machinery without allocating real memory. On a single-node deployment this worked: the placeholder ran, the batch finished, and the client received an error.

In disaggregated mode such as we operate, the admission queues on both prefill and decode checked whether a request was finished, not whether it was rejected. A rejected request reported itself as live. So:

  1. Bootstrap. The router told the decode node the prompt length (8 pages in the diagram). Decode reserved 8 KV pages for the request.
  2. Prefill admission. The prefill admission queue admitted any request where req.finished() was False. A rejected request stored its rejection in to_finish, not finished_reason, so finished() still returned False. The rejected request was admitted.
  3. Prefill forward pass. Rejection had already replaced the prompt with a one-token placeholder. Prefill ran a trivial forward pass on that one token.
  4. KV transfer. Prefill sent one page of KV to decode and signaled that the transfer was complete.
  5. Decode admission. Decode's admission queue had the same finished() check, so it accepted the handoff.
  6. Decode attention. Decode started generating and attention read all 8 reserved pages. Only page P0 had been written by this request. Pages P1 to P7 still held what earlier requests left in them: other users' prompts and partial generations.
  7. Response. The client got HTTP 200 instead of HTTP 400. prompt_tokens matched the long prompt and the reply was coherent. It arrived faster than an 8-page prefill should take, and it contained content from other users' KV pages.

Every request over the threshold behaved this way. This bug had been reported to SGLang by another user as issue #30233 on July 6, 2026, which Cloudflare noticed while investigating this incident. We had been flagging these types of issues with SGLang since v0.5.10 and this security incident sped up work that Cloudflare had already started in collaboration with the SGLang team. The patch for this issue was released in SGLang v0.5.20, with follow-ups in v0.5.21 and v0.5.22, and is available for all other operators dependent on SGLang to use. We highly recommend all operators update SGLang dependencies to v0.5.22 or later. For more details on specific PRs, read on below.

GLM 5.3 was the only model affected by this bug. Every other disaggregated deployment on Workers AI has KV pools larger than its context length on both prefill and decode, so no request could reach the rejection path. We have applied the engine fix and the hardening described below to every model we serve with SGLang, and our deployment checks require them for every new deployment.

Timeline

All times UTC.

When

What

Aug 27, 2026

GLM 5.3 launched on Workers AI with a prefill KV pool smaller than its context window. The exposure was present from launch.

Sep 8, 2026 - 23:11

Report received via HackerOne.

Sep 9, 2026 - 08:00

Cloudflare begins verifying the HackerOne report.

Sep 9, 2026 - 13:22

Security incident declared. Product Security reproduced the leak using two independent accounts within 25 minutes.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:00

After confirming the scope of the issue, GLM 5.3 was set to private. Requests return HTTP 400. Status page updated.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:35

Root cause identified as the prefill pool being smaller than the context length. Canary prefill node with a larger pool confirmed not susceptible.

Sep 9, 2026 - 14:52

All prefill nodes rolled to the corrected configuration.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:04

Full deployment rebuilt with the corrected configuration plus a Cloudflare-authored engine patch that correctly returns errors for requests rejected by the prefill scheduler. Validated against the researcher's reproduction script.

Sep 9, 2026 - 19:40

Model restored to public.

Sep 10, 2026 - 23:30

Meeting with the SGLang maintainers (RadixArk CTO and core engineers) to agree on upstream fixes.

Sep 11-19, 2026

Additional hardening rolled to all production SGLang deployments (details below).

Sep 16-Oct 12, 2026

Upstream SGLang merges the admission fix, per-transfer checksums, abort-ACK preservation, and turns deferred KV release on by default.

Oct 2, 2026

SGLang v0.5.21 released.

Oct 19, 2026

SGLang v0.5.22 released.

Oct 26, 2026

Coordinated publication with the researcher and RadixArk.

Ongoing hardening effort

This bug belongs to a class of KV cache memory-safety bugs that Cloudflare has been working to address for several months. In each case, a page is freed, reused, or read while something else still has a claim on it. We see two common causes.

The first is page lifetime within a single node. Several tasks on a decode node can hold the same page at once: token generation, offload to host memory, the KV transfer receiver, and the abort and error paths. If one of them frees the page while another is still using it, a new request can be given that page while it is still being read or written. Our earlier fixes for decode offload (#24226, #30899) and double release on grammar errors (#30937) were of this kind.

The second is a race across nodes. When a request is aborted while prefill is still writing its KV cache to decode over RDMA, the writes already sent cannot be recalled. If decode frees those pages right away, those pages can be given to another request, and the late writes land in that request's KV cache. Cloudflare has contributed to the effort to fix this race through proposed fixes (#31357, #38961) and a reproduction script (#32564). In both cases the result is corrupted output, or one user's data in another user's response, with no error raised. The bug in this incident was different: a rejected request went through the handoff every time, rather than by a timing accident. But it had the same result: decode reading pages this request never wrote. None of these covered the failure in this incident in which prefill rejected the request, and decode never learned of it.

Since the incident, we have:

  • Extended deferred release to hold prefill's source pages as well, and to cover every failure type, not just aborts. We proposed it upstream as #38961, which was superseded by #40645, #41402, and #41404.
  • Deployed bounded Mooncake transfer batches (#32758, from the SGLang community), so no single transfer call can outlast the release timeout.
  • Changed our load balancer so a client disconnect no longer aborts a request mid-transfer. It holds the prefill connection until prefill finishes and the decode connection until the first token, then closes both.
  • Added a check to every disaggregated deployment change: KV pool size measured against context length, deferred release on both roles, transfer batch bounds inside the release timeout, and all required patches applied.

All of these changes were released to our disaggregated production deployments.

Working with the SGLang team

We met with the SGLang maintainers at RadixArk on September 10, the day after the incident. We agreed that RadixArk would investigate the race conditions we had reported, upstream the integrity-checking idea, and build reproduction tests for this class of bug.

The following have landed on SGLang main to address this incident and related KV cache race conditions, and all but one are included in v0.5.22. Operators running disaggregated SGLang should update to v0.5.22 or backport these patches as needed. 

Category

Pull request

Release

What it does

Incident

#36988

v0.5.20

Retires aborted prefill requests before their result reaches decode. This stops the exposure in this incident.

Incident

#38935

v0.5.21

Rejects these requests at admission, before any bootstrap, allocation, or KV transfer. Follows the approach in Cloudflare's draft patch, #38704.

Race

#39461, #41612

v0.5.21, v0.5.22

sgl-router cancels both halves of a request on client disconnect or prefill failure.

Race

#37454, #41023

v0.5.20, v0.5.21

Enables deferred KV release only on backends that support it, then turns it on by default.

Race

#40645, #41402

v0.5.21

Fixes cases where the drain confirmation was lost, so releases happen on confirmation instead of waiting out the timeout.

Race

#41404

v0.5.21

Holds pages on every transfer failure, not only decode-initiated aborts.

Race

#41618

v0.5.21

Fixes a regression in the abort notification path.

Race

#43719

v0.5.22

A failed Mooncake send no longer reports its writes as drained.

Race

#37077

v0.5.22

Tags abort messages per request so a reused ID cannot consume a stale confirmation. Adds MORI support.

Race

#36612

v0.5.20

Shares the prefill-to-decode failure notification across Mooncake, NIXL, and MORI.

Race

#32758

v0.5.20

Optional cap on Mooncake transfer batch size, so one timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded number of writes in flight.

Lifetime

#30899

v0.5.21

Decode waits for an in-progress offload to host memory before retracting a request and freeing its pages. Authored by Cloudflare.

Lifetime

#43562

v0.5.22

Keeps tensor-parallel ranks in agreement when a host-memory cache restore fails.

Observability

#39500

v0.5.21

Adds --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum: decode verifies a checksum of the transferred KV before generating. Cleanup in #39729, merged and awaiting release.

Observability

#38596, #40642

v0.5.20, v0.5.21

Fixes for SGLang's KV canary, which detects and logs potential corruption.

Observability

#41128

v0.5.22

Metrics for deferred release: count, duration, and whether each hold ended on drain confirmation or timeout.

These follow-ups are still works in progress:

  • #39729 Additional cleanup for --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum. Merged, awaiting release.
  • Zero KV pages on release, draft proposal: #46435
  • Extend KV checksum validation from the prefill-to-decode handoff to every decode step (see Integrity by construction, below)
  • Broader KV Canary and KV Checksum model and feature support

What we recommend to other operators

If you run SGLang in disaggregated prefill/decode mode, we recommend the following:

  1. Measure your KV pool and compare it to your context length, on every prefill and decode node, from the engine's startup log, after every change to weights, quantization, parallelism, or memory fraction. If the pool is smaller, lower the context length to fit. Do not rely on a proxy to enforce the limit, and do not assume the engine will reject what does not fit. This is the check we did not enforce.
  2. Upgrade to a build that includes #36988 and #38935 (v0.5.22 or later), so an over-length request is rejected before handoff regardless of pool size. This is the engine-side fix, and it is the backstop for the day your check in step one is wrong.
  3. Run with deferred KV release on both roles (default after #41023), and bound your Mooncake transfer batches so a single timed-out call cannot leave an unbounded tail of writes.
  4. Turn on corruption detection where your model supports it. --disaggregation-enable-kv-checksum and --kv-canary do not yet cover every model architecture. Check your logs to confirm requests are being verified. We are working with the SGLang team to extend both checks to more architectures, including GLM 5.3, GLM 5.3 Flash, and DeepSeek V4.
  5. Ensure your proxy is not generating unnecessary aborts. Configure your load balancer to allow requests to proceed up to the first token, so that you do not trigger an abort that requires cross-node coordination.

Longer term

Integrity by construction

Configuration checks and lifecycle fixes reduce the number of ways a page can be misused. They do not make misuse impossible, and this incident is a reminder that the next bug will have a shape we have not seen. The durable answer is for the engine to detect, at read time, that a request is about to attend over a page it does not own, and fail that one request rather than return someone else's data.

We built a prototype of this over the summer and described it in August. Every physical KV page carries a tag that changes when the page is reallocated, each request records the tags it expects, and the mapping is checked before decode reads the cache. In our tests it cost under 1% in throughput and tail latency. We tested it on GLM 5.2 in mid-August, but disabled it shortly afterwards due to reliability issues.

The prototype was also tied to specific attention backends and model architectures, so it could not be a general fix. We are working with the SGLang team to build a production version into the engine that works across every model, rather than maintaining Cloudflare-specific patches. The per-transfer checksum in #39500 is a first step: it validates the handoff from prefill to decode. Page-level tags go further, because they check every read, including reads long after the transfer.

Integrity by mathematical impossibility

RDMA copies data directly from one node’s memory to another’s. It’s vital for the two machines to agree on where the data goes, how large it is, and when it’s finished; any mismatch can cause the receiver to read the wrong data. This bug is an example of a consistency failure in a distributed system, in which the two machines had inconsistent views of the state of that system.

Elsewhere in Cloudflare, we have put effort into proving the safety of distributed systems using formal verification methods. Topaz enables conflict-free IP selection for our authoritative DNS servers. Models of Meerkat’s QuePaxa implementation have demonstrated consistency bugs that were subsequently fixed.

We are now directing our experience in formal methods to KV cache transfer engines. This will start with modeling and proving the safety of an RDMA-based KV cache transfer protocol. The goal is to model our production SGLang’s distributed KV cache system using Mooncake, then track and fix any divergence from the safety properties we want to guarantee. The aim is to prove — as far as possible — that a bug like this cannot occur again. Realistically, we expect gaps in what the provers can tell us, but proving the rest of the system allows us to more closely review and monitor those gaps.

Coordinated disclosure

We are publishing this report as part of a coordinated disclosure. We want to thank the researcher, Gadi Evron, who reported this through our HackerOne program with a clear, reproducible script and gave us time to fix it and to coordinate with the SGLang maintainers before publishing. We also want to thank the SGLang team at RadixArk, who treated this as their problem as well as ours and landed the upstream fixes with urgency.

Read more at the post from the SGLang team.

If you find a security issue in Workers AI, please report it at hackerone.com/cloudflare.

item.title: 26th October – Threat Intelligence Report
item.description:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 26th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin. TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES Japanese cloud hosting provider Onamae Desktop Cloud has confirmed a cyberattack in which intruders compromised its infrastructure and installed malware on customer servers. More than 26,000 servers were potentially affected. The provider […]

The post 26th October – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 26th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.

TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

  • Japanese cloud hosting provider Onamae Desktop Cloud has confirmed a cyberattack in which intruders compromised its infrastructure and installed malware on customer servers. More than 26,000 servers were potentially affected. The provider began shutting down customer environments on October 21 to contain the intrusion and prevent further unauthorized activity.
  • India’s state-run State Bank of India, serving more than 500 million customers, disclosed a data breach after 3,897 customer records appeared online. The exposed information reportedly included contact details, residential addresses, birth dates, bank profiles, loan records, and identity-verification documents. The bank reported no disruption to core services.
  • WordPress backup developer TeamUpdraft has suffered a cyberattack after intruders accessed its website and potentially exposed customer information and management-service connection keys. Attackers subsequently abused compromised UpdraftCentral keys to install backdoors on WordPress websites during an 18-hour campaign on October 18 and 19.
  • LiteLLM, a widely used open-source AI gateway, confirmed an October 21 supply-chain attack in which attackers used stolen developer tokens to publish malicious packages and Docker images. The compromised version 1.107.0 was designed to steal cloud credentials and AI service secrets, with attackers subsequently testing stolen AWS credentials.

AI THREATS

  • Check Point Research uncovered how AI-enabled antidetect browsers allow operators to manage thousands of deceptive accounts while evading platform safeguards. Tools including Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin facilitate account takeovers, financial fraud, and automated distribution of AI-generated content, supporting large-scale influence operations across social media platforms.
  • Researchers observed affiliates of INC and The Gentlemen ransomware groups using AI agents to conduct human-approved cyberattacks. The operation targeted 62 organizations by exploiting remote-access systems and compromised credentials. Victims were concentrated in the manufacturing, energy, healthcare, and pharmaceutical sectors, primarily in the United States.
  • Researchers analyzed a cybercriminal operation that used multiple AI assistants to plan and execute different types of malicious activity. The attacker relied on AI-generated scripts and reconnaissance reports to develop attack capabilities. Exposed operational records revealed how AI tools supported campaign planning, technical execution, and adaptation across different targets.

VULNERABILITIES AND PATCHES

  • Critical PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 have been used in widespread exploitation attempts that could enable remote code execution. Attack traffic reportedly increased from thousands to millions of attempts following disclosure. As of October 23, approximately 97.5% of publicly visible PHP instances did not indicate patched versions.

Check Point IPS provides protection against this threat (PHP Remote Code Execution (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619, CVE-2026-115560((

  • Oracle has released its October 2026 Critical Patch Update, addressing 1,209 unique vulnerabilities through 1,295 security patches across 33 product families. The update includes 95 critical CVEs and affects widely deployed enterprise products, including Fusion Middleware, E-Business Suite, MySQL, and Java SE.
  • GitLab has fixed CVE-2026-110264, a critical vulnerability with a CVSS score of 10.0 affecting Community and Enterprise Editions. The integer overflow flaw could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely on affected servers. The vulnerability affects versions before 18.11.13 and several 19.x releases.
  • A critical privilege-escalation vulnerability, CVE-2026-114625, affects on-premises Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 9.4 and allows authenticated users, including those with read-only access, to obtain operator-level permissions. Successful exploitation can expose restricted management functions, and the vulnerability has been exploited in attacks.

THREAT INTELLIGENCE REPORTS

  • Check Point Research has profiled Aokigahara, a newly identified infostealer targeting credentials and session data associated with AI applications, developer tools, and cloud platforms. Targeted applications include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot. Stolen information may include authentication tokens, account credentials, and other sensitive application data.
  • Researchers revealed that U.S. federal investigators suspect an executive at a ransomware negotiation company assisted the ShinyHunters extortion group in operating its victim disclosure website. The site reportedly listed nearly 100 organizations between May and October 2026.
  • Researchers mapped Lazarus’s Operation FlashHole, a cyberespionage campaign targeting organizations in South Korea’s software, construction, and telecommunications equipment sectors. Attackers used tailored phishing messages and fraudulent portfolio websites to deliver malware. The campaign exploited trusted financial-security software to execute malicious components.
  • Researchers have uncovered a large-scale campaign by threat actor k0t targeting Fortinet FortiGate, FortiWeb, and Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect devices. Attackers exploited vulnerabilities and weak credentials to establish persistent access and steal information. The operation exposed more than 70,000 credentials and showed possible connections to ransomware groups.

The post 26th October – Threat Intelligence Report appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.description:
Interesting research:

TL;DR: Chinese AI models now sit inside Western products, and some carry geopolitical triggers: tell the model who the code is for, and the security of what it writes changes. For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it.

  • One word tilts the code against Americans. Ask for the app “for a US defense contractor” instead of “for a Chinese defense contractor”, and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked. ...
item.content:encoded:
Interesting research:

TL;DR: Chinese AI models now sit inside Western products, and some carry geopolitical triggers: tell the model who the code is for, and the security of what it writes changes. For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it.

  • One word tilts the code against Americans. Ask for the app “for a US defense contractor” instead of “for a Chinese defense contractor”, and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked.
  • Hong Kong’s democracy movement gets apps that leak. Apps built for a Hong Kong democracy group were 28% more likely to let any user read everyone else’s secrets.
  • Asking for secure code didn’t help. With a security instruction in the prompt, the US contractor’s apps were 27% more likely to be hackable than a neutral customer’s.
  • Westernized Qwen3-Coder closed all three gaps. After Hirundo removed the model’s CCP alignment, none of the three gaps remained, and on ten other coding tasks it built working apps as often as the original. It is available on Hugging Face.

I would like more details on how the bias was removed.

item.title: Looking for a Language [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 21st)
item.description: [This is a Guest Diary by Jeffray Spence, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a Guest Diary by Jeffray Spence, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Around Here, we start our day with coffee, but our day does not begin until we have our data...So much data.  Where to even begin?

When approaching a massive dataset, such as those from a DShield SIEM Honeypot, the first step is to actually find something to analyze.  As for myself, I usually go looking for something that makes me go; "Huh."

Today we will be walking through a starting approach with Kibana Discover to search out embedded language preferences in webtraffic, then we will use this as a starting point for finding anomalous activity.

Find A Problem to Get Some Data

Inside of my DShield SIEM there are nearly a million records, so I approach by looking for a slightly smaller data carve with which to work which still represents the problem set:

Anyone with Elastic Kibana can perform this approach on their webtraffic data as long as the HTTP headers are provided.  Here, the logs are from my SANS Dshield Honeypot and the accompanying Dshield SIEM.  For those who desire to install this setup there are plenty of great resources out there with links at the end of this article [1] [2].

In slightly more than 3 weeks of observation the rasperry pi honeypot had transferred a Million Records into the Elastic SIEM.  These many records can prove very challenging when figuring out where to start, so it is helpful to know that even with no filtering applied on the Discover page the Field Statistics will give some fairly detailed metrics about what fields exist in the current Index.

On the Discover page in the upper right, I selected my index (here the index is “cowrie”) and without any filter applied I selected Field Statistics:

Calculating statistics ourselves is possible using ESQL and Stats, however this feature of Elastic makes gaining visibility much more obtainable at the onset.  We are immediately presented with a screen displaying all of the Documents broken down by Top Values which potentially gives us some valuable insight:

The resultant statistics show that in these 3 weeks my honeypot had generated 960,000 logs, but all of those are only within 4 rules.  Four is less than a 960,000 so this gives a more manageable starting dataset:

“Huh.”  This little raspberry PI has been humming away quietly all day and all night and only 4 rules have popped up.  I found this interesting.  With no filtering applied only 15,271 records triggered any rule?

This setup is a honeypot, so literally every record is suspicious.  So, what about the other 944,866 records which triggered no rules?

Today, we want a problem not a project, so we are going to use one of these rules to narrow down our traffic for analysis.

We have rule triggers for the Index page.  Boring.  Great for generating a large dataset, but this is not a very targeted approach.

Git Config is something I had previously analyzed, and this led me to discover malicious traffic attempting to scrape Git Config from internet hosts.  Neat, but not for today.

Fortinet Emulation, for those who don't know, has fairly recently gotten a lot of attention [3].
Only one detection so far in my honeypot, so for me that's just an outlier.  Interesting, but not much of a corpus.

Through the process of elimination, we are left with the Sonicwall Appliance Login Page rule.
Good representation over the problem space with 41 individual hosts logging in activity.  This could potentially demonstrate how an attack is conducted or give a clue as to who was conducting one.  Perfect because we are looking for regular and repeating attack attempts.  I selected these criteria as a Kibana filter.

Now to start digging.

Data Selection

Now that we have a smaller dataset to work within, we need to decide what we want to find.  After that we need to figure out how to actually find that.

This first approach is what I would NOT recommend One do:

Noticing here that every field statistic for all 157 records has One Distinct Value and only1 category under Distribution tells us these fields are ALL common to ALL records.  A field common to every record will have a unique value for each record. 

We don't want common, we want weird: the approach I will use is to flip it and look at Distribution 2 or higher.  This is Long tail analysis:

Here we see the Distinct values are now descending with the “sweet spot” between 2 and 6 so.  Not an exact criterion, but one that is practical for manual review.

Within these fields we have fields of interest:

When fields contain similar values, they may illustrate a relationship between the data represented.  Here the traffic triggering the Sonicwall Rule contains a relatively small subset of unique values.  The next step is to find something we cannot readily explain away; a simple exercise to conduct on the “tags”, “host.ip”, and “host.mac” fields.  The IP and MAC are going to be both interfaces of my Dshield Pi itself, while the Tags are going to be metadata about how the rules generate.  The “source.geo.continent_code” is not very useful in a Virtual Private Server (VPS) enabled world but may prove useful later.  This leaves 2 fields:

http.request.connection

"Close" and "close".  Most traffic parsing tools are going to convert these all to lowercase string, and thus never see this small difference.
.  No longer interesting.

http.request.mime_type

"utf-8" (the defacto choice) verses some interesting mime encoding...

Next was to break down what this mime encoding is saying: "GBK,utf-8;q=0.7,*;q=0.3"

This string is sent to a webserver as the Accept-Charset HTTP header.  Values of GBK,utf-8, and wildcard (*) are present.  The preference weights are specified as "q" (for “quality value” by convention).  Since the implicit maximum weight value is q=1.0, the simplified character set preferences are:

(GBK;q=1.0),(utf-8;q=0.7),(*;q=0.3)

I think of this as a preference for what character encoding to use: 
(Send me “GBK” 100% of the time, if not “utf-8” 70%, and if not Whatever 30%)

UTF-8 makes sense as does wildcard (*).  However, GBK is explicitly the extension of the “GB 2312” character set for Simplified Chinese characters.
"Huh."

Why do these requests explicitly state they greatly desire to transfer data to my Honeypot, which is not in China, using an exclusively Chinese character set?
I also apply this as a filter in Kibana to narrow our results to 8 Records:


 
Two issues are now present.  This dataset of 8 records is too narrow to work with, and also, we don’t actually care about the Sonicwall rule anymore now that we find some interesting traffic.  Next, we need to pull in some additional data for this mime type field.

Finding commonality

So my Elastic SIEM, the webhoneypot index is for Webserver Logs, and my cowrie index shares these fields.  Here the filter works for both.
At this point we are not interested in the “Sonicwall Appliance” filter anymore, so we remove it.  We are now using the “Mime Type” field to work out the language preferences and have 47 interesting records within the http.request.mime_type:

These records now represent every inbound connection attempt sending this exact same format string for the GBK Character set preferences.  There are 47 requests in total which send the identical preference header.  How can we use this header to find odd traffic in our data?

The problem set has not changed, only our dataset.  We repeat the same process of sorting the Distribution Field under the Field statistics section.

Following this Distribution Analysis process we see two User-Agents, which is interesting.
However, we also very clearly see there are two source.geo.region_name values:

“Beijing”, yeah, ok that makes sense. Beijing is in China… but “Ontario”?

"Huh".  People do move around, however, following a purely statistical analysis approach one would not anticipate that Canadian Cyber actors would greatly desire a Chinese Character set while targeting my American Honeypot.  This presents as an anomaly.

We add the source.geo.region_name: Ontario filter and observe there are now only 3 records:

At this point I exported these three records to Libre Office so I could look at them:

Modern VPS availability makes the Autonomous System (AS) number far more useful than an IP: AS-7456 is the system responsible for all three of these records.  
This field, “source.geo.as.number” will be our next field to analyze:

What’s Your Number?

We now set our new filter to be source.geo.as.number: 7456
We remove all other filters and follow the same “Distribution Analysis” as before.  We immediately find the same pattern:

There is again a language preference but this time in a different field:
The http.request.accept-language encoding for all 31 requests from AS-7456 read as either:

zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.628 at (90.3%)
OR
zh-CN,zh;q=0.83 at (9.7%)

"zh-CN" means "Mainland Chinese" Language preference.
"zh" just means any version of Chinese.

For all 121 records observed for this AS there were 31 alternative language preference specified.
This is an optional header, however the indication of a desired alternate language preference can narrow down our search scope considerably.  

I applied the filter as:

http.request.accept-language: "zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.6" OR http.request.accept-language: "zh-CN,zh;q=0.8"

At this point I exported the 31 records for this filter:

I took these records over to LibreOffice as a Tab Separated Value sheet so I could have a look at it.
When I did the pattern was unmistakable:

These are all regularly scanning internet hosts for the same set of endpoints all from the same Canadian based AS-7456:

165[.]154.36.91
165[.]154.29.93
165[.]154.11.140
165[.]154.120.226
165[.]154.33.72
165[.]154.182.221

Values for http.request.body.content were all consistent repetitions of:

/cgi-bin/login
/config.json
/sitemap.xml
/robots.txt
/favicon.ico
/

There is no attempt being made to conceal the fact that these user agents strongly desire Chinese character sets in the HTTP Language preferences while actively targeting internet facing endpoints.  We have discovered an obviously automated campaign.

Interestingly, tzrhxln[.]cn (165[.]154.29.93) is a suspect high entropy domain.
Similar domains also appear in this dataset as extracted with this ESQL Query:

source.domain values:
  leheedu[.]cn
  mail.,brossy.com[.]cn
  mail.brossy.com[.]cn
  tzrhxln[.]cn

All of these domains operate from AS-7456, have strong CN presence, and are actively scanning.

One Conclusion

This demonstration of a simple approach to Elastic Discovery using optional HTTP language preferences and mime types is only an example.  We have found high entropy domains, bot scanners, and plenty of nefarious intent, however the most interesting aspect in my view is the approach we have taken.  Expanding upon this could yield automation.

Typically, when analyzing datasets in a SIEM it is common to look for all the fields that match a correlation.  In this approach we attempt to match the least commonality required to gain a single insight into what hosts may be related and then repeat the data acquisition process with this selected feature.  This is featuring selection, and because we are purposely iterating upon the selection with intent, we are functionally engaged in rudimentary feature engineering.

Using the embedded language preferences in webtraffic as a starting point we were able to trim a massive corpus into a manageable selection.  We have also built upon some understanding of how these language headers appear in logs when browsing, so we could always simply begin selecting those features as a starting point in the future when processing SIEM data.

Just a simple example for today, but we eventually found what we were looking for.  Also, most importantly, the more efficient we are in the search, then the more time we have for our coffee.

[1] https://github.com/dshield-isc/dshield
[2] https://github.com/bruneaug/DShield-SIEM
[3] https://www.fortinet.com/blog/psirt-blogs/analysis-of-reported-credential-compromise-of-fortigate-devices
[4] https://www.sans.edu/cyber-security-programs/bachelors-degree/

-----------
Guy Bruneau IPSS Inc.
My GitHub Page
Twitter: GuyBruneau
gbruneau at isc dot sans dot edu
