item.title: Can’t Patch PHP2Shell Yet? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
item.description: Executive Summary PHP2Shell’s fix is to update PHP, but patching at scale is slow. Only 199,000 of 156 million PHP installations were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure. In the meantime, Qualys’s configuration-level mitigation reduces exposure to the confirmed attack path without code changes, with or without an agent. WAF, IPS, and EDR […]
item.content:encoded:
Executive Summary

PHP2Shell’s fix is to update PHP, but patching at scale is slow. Only 199,000 of 156 million PHP installations were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure. In the meantime, Qualys’s configuration-level mitigation reduces exposure to the confirmed attack path without code changes, with or without an agent. WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers, and TruConfirm shows which hosts are actually reachable: 25 of 1,539 in one customer environment. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but patching remains the only complete fix.

PHP2Shell comes with a clear instruction: update PHP. Fixed releases exist for supported branches. Patching at this scale still takes time. In Qualys telemetry, only 199,000 of the 156 million PHP package installations with a known version (about 0.13%) had been patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while updates roll out, and the right visibility shows which servers need attention first. Our PHP2Shell blog post covers detection and fixed versions.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and patch, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed PHP, apply the Qualys mitigation, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed PHP

Qualys customers can identify PHP installations through network scans, Cloud Agents, container assessments, and Deep Scan, where supported. Additionally, they can assess exposed web applications and APIs using Qualys TotalAppSec. To facilitate PHP discovery, use QID 45110, followed by the relevant vulnerability-detection QIDs and software-inventory QIDs, to assess the assets in scope.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable host has the same level of exposure. TruConfirm helps validate the indicators of the tested PHP2Shell entry point. Its benign probe checks whether this entry point is reachable and whether the upload-progress mitigation is absent, all without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure. For more details, refer to our PHP2Shell blog post, which explains how the probe works.

In one customer environment with 1,539 assets running PHP, TruConfirm returned positive validation results for 25 of those assets. Consider these results alongside their internet exposure and business criticality to determine what vulnerabilities to prioritize for mitigation and patching. Keep in mind that a negative result does not guarantee that all exploitation paths are closed.

Step 2: Apply the Qualys Mitigation

Qualys provides a configuration-level mitigation for PHP2Shell based on PHP’s guidance and insights from the Qualys Threat Research Unit. It turns off session upload progress and hardens related session-handling configuration on supported hosts. This reduces exposure to the confirmed session-lifecycle attack path without requiring application-code changes. 

It does not eliminate every exploitation path associated with the two CVEs. Test applications that depend on upload-progress functionality after the change.

  • With or without an agent. Customers with vulnerable detections can select Mitigate Now from their dashboards. For appliances, DMZ servers, and legacy hosts that cannot run a Cloud Agent, the same mitigation script is available in the Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) library in TruRisk Eliminate and runs directly on scanner-based hosts.
  • Configuration-level, with restart verification. The mitigation applies configuration changes and automatically restarts the PHP service. Review the execution logs and restart the service manually if a restart is still required. Confirm that every affected PHP worker has picked up the new configuration.
  • Verified, not assumed. After the restart, Qualys checks the effective configuration to confirm the setting is active and not overridden elsewhere.

Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the mitigation, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses

Inbound: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Akamai, Cloudflare, F5, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, and Check Point have released signatures that name both CVEs. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach PHP. Cloudflare has reported attack traffic that includes evasion attempts, so treat signatures as one of several layers.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a web server process launching a shell or dropping a web shell.

PHP2Shell 3rd-party mitigation and compensating controls

Select the WAF, IPS, and EDR you run to see the exact signatures and policies each vendor has released for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, ready to copy into your console.

  1. Edge

    WAF

    None

  2. Network

    IPS

    None

  3. Host

    EDR

    None

    Platform

Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation and are mapped to the attacker’s next step, not to the CVEs themselves, so verify each one fires for your PHP worker. Compensating controls reduce risk; updating PHP remains the only complete fix.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Mitigation reduces risk in the interim. Updating remains the only complete fix. You can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate. Qualys reports a High patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for this PHP package update.

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

  1. Restart every service that loads PHP.
  2. Verify the installed packages and that running PHP workers are on the patched build.
  3. Repeat TruConfirm validation and verify the effective configuration. Do the same after applying the mitigation in Step 2.

Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM

The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change.

Two servers can run the same unpatched PHP build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule that names both CVEs, with EDR watching its web server process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps:

  1. Recommendations on every finding (coming in Q4). ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where.
  2. Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention.
  3. Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate from the platform that found the exposure.

Where to Start

  1. Find. Use QID 45110 to support PHP discovery to detect CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, then use the applicable vulnerability detection QIDs and software inventory to assess assets in scope.
  2. Use TruConfirm results alongside internet exposure and business criticality to prioritize remediation. 
  3. Mitigate. Apply the Qualys mitigation to systems awaiting an update, using agent-based or scanner-based execution as applicable. Verify the effective configuration and required restarts. 
  4. Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers.
  5. Patch and verify. Deploy the PHP or vendor update, restart every service that loads PHP, verify that the patched build is running, and repeat the relevant validation checks.

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

Not a Qualys customer? Access Qualys’ free PHP2Shell mitigation service to help protect your environment against this threat.

Sign Up for Free Mitigation Service

item.title: How to Identify Compromised eMudhra Certificates With Qualys (CVE-2026-111943)
item.description: Executive Summary A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, […]
item.content:encoded:
Executive Summary

A critical certificate authority incident disclosed on October 17, 2026, impacts eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. A flaw in the key generation process could allow attackers to recover private keys and issue fraudulent TLS or code-signing certificates. The affected intermediates have been revoked and blocked by major platform vendors, including Chrome, Mozilla, Apple, and Microsoft. The issue is tracked as CVE-2026-111943.

The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported recovering the private keys for eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates after discovering that the underlying cryptographic keys contained only a fraction of the expected entropy. Browser and OS vendors have since blocked the certificates, and eMudhra has revoked them. Security teams now face an immediate question: Where do certificates issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediates exist within my environment?

Qualys VMDR and Qualys Certificate View already collect the data needed to answer that. This post explains how to use them, with QQL queries you can run today.

What is eMudhra?

eMudhra, a digital trust and cybersecurity provider, offers solutions spanning Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), digital certificates, identity management, and secure digital transactions. Recent security concerns involving eight of its intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates highlight the importance of strong cryptographic key generation, rigorous validation, and continuous oversight of digital trust infrastructure. The incident reinforces a critical security lesson: trust in digital certificates depends not just on the technology, but on the operational controls protecting the keys behind them.

What Happened

A flaw in eMudhra’s key generation process produced a second set of weak P-384 keys during a wrap/unwrap step, and those weak keys were mistakenly used for eight intermediate CA certificates. This flaw reduced the effective entropy of the affected P-384 keys to an estimated 3 to 8 bits, making private-key recovery trivial to compute.

The weak keys came from a key generation ceremony held on April 30, 2025, for 24 subordinate CAs. Anyone holding the private key of one of these intermediates could issue a certificate that impersonates any website or service, subject to each client’s validation controls. Some key points about the incident:

  • Six of the eight intermediates are TLS CAs; two are code-signing CAs.
  • Browsers: Chrome, Mozilla, and Apple have blocked the TLS certificates, and Microsoft has blocked the two code-signing certificates.
  • Root distrust: Google removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from the Chrome Root Store, and Mozilla removed trust in the root that signed the intermediates.
  • eMudhra: has revoked the eight certificates and stopped issuing new certificates under its G3 root. It states that its root CA private keys and other intermediate CAs are not affected, and that the issue is limited to its global website-security business, not Indian DSC and eSign services.
  • Exploitation: eMudhra says only one of the affected intermediates was used in production, and none of them issued certificates to websites or end users.

Who is at Most Risk?

Organizations should prioritize investigation if they:

  • Operate internet-facing websites, APIs, VPNs, or other TLS-enabled services.
  • Use publicly trusted certificates issued through eMudhra or emSign trust hierarchies.
  • Distribute signed software that relies on publicly trusted code-signing certificates.
  • Develop or run applications built on the Go programming language.
  • Maintain legacy systems, unmanaged endpoints, or custom trust stores that may not receive certificate distrust updates automatically.

The Eight Affected Intermediate Certificates

The table below lists the certificates identified. The SHA-256 fingerprint and serial number are the most reliable identifiers when you search your inventory.

How Can Qualys VMDR and Certificate View Help Identify eMudhra Certificates?

Use Certificate View, included with VMDR, to identify certificates issued by affected eMudhra authorities and use VMDR with Cloud Agent to identify hosts running vulnerable Go installations or software requiring vendor-issued updates.

Step 1: Make Sure Coverage Is Complete

  • Entitle Certificate View on your VMDR scan ranges. Confirm that the IP ranges you scan with VMDR are enabled in Certificate View.
  • Add external domains. For sites hosted by web or app providers, add the FQDNs or IP addresses in Certificate View. It runs a lightweight scan across standard ports to detect TLS services and analyze their certificates.
  • Use Cloud Agent where scans cannot reach. Agents report software and certificate data from endpoints, servers, and remote workers that network scans miss.

Step 2: Pinpoint the Eight Compromised Intermediates

To confirm whether any of the eight compromised intermediates appear in a chain, search for their SHA-256 fingerprints, serial numbers, or issuer names in Certificate View > Certificates.

Reference QQL Queries

By Issuer:

certificate:(issuer.name:[`EM EV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3B`, `EM EV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM DV TLS CA – G3C`, `EM OV CS CA – G3B`, `EM OV CS CA – G3C`])

By Serial Number:

certificate:(serialNumber:`c7c41efe92d825f05eae841a4a82c1` or serialNumber:`6cada367fb1c100088120ea202d568` or serialNumber:`a4aee678f23362b4c0e460b772f214` or serialNumber:`8009928a64107601af05fa2f19f109` or serialNumber:`296926c227a3a1526392b19482a504` or serialNumber:`588b2e3c2bb8cda13e1a1209254321` or serialNumber:`7818933f8f85b4619a2b35fba83d0a` or serialNumber:`544b7f922c31ae220a4a922916f6e6`)

The Information tab shows the fingerprints, serial number, and first and last found dates so that you can compare them with the SHA-256 values in the table.

Step 3: Find Software That Still Trusts the Affected Certificates

Certificates presented by your servers are only half of the exposure. Applications running older Go runtimes may continue to trust certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates. VMDR/Cloud Agent can help you find them.

Find Go toolchains to update

Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 block certificate chains that contain any of the eight compromised keys (CVE-2026-111943). Qualys has released QID 5019897 for SwCA scanning to detect affected Go versions. Before you scan, confirm your agents have the latest signatures that include this QID, so the new scan picks it up. Then open the Vulnerabilities tab and use the query below to list the impacted assets:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:5019897

Find Additional Vendor-Specific Updates

Qualys has also released QIDs to detect Go vulnerabilities associated with other vendor operating systems.

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:[364203,364206,364213,364219,364220,364229,364251,364253,364264,364268,364270,364299,364332,364333,45804,290608,290616,711201,766002,766003,766006,766008,945683,945690,945699,945727,945728,945732,945742,945745,945746,945749,964523,964525,964554,964555,964557,964558,964566,964567,964570,5019897,6056475,6056480,6056489,6056500,6056501,6056505,6056506,6056513,6056514,6056520,6056530,6056535,6056537,6056540,6056541,6056542,6056545,6056546,6056551,6056552,6056553,6056556,6056562,6056565,6056570,6056573,6056574,6056575,6601013,6601015,6601022,6601033,6601039,6601042,6601047,6601053,6601071,6601073,6601077,6601079,6601080,6601081,6666650,6684005,6684017,6684042]

Enumerate Affected eMudhra Certificate Chains

In addition to software detection, Qualys is releasing QID 48395: eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates Enumeration. This Information Gathered (IG) QID helps identify systems presenting or using certificate chains that contain the affected eMudhra intermediate CA certificates. Once available in your subscription, you can query for assets using:

vulnerabilities.vulnerability.qid:48395

Optional Check: Find eMudhra-Issued Certificates with QQL Queries in Certificate View

Open Certificate View > Certificates, paste the query below into the search bar, and run it. It matches any certificate whose issuer organization is one of the eMudhra entities in the affected list.

certificate:(issuer.organization:`eMudhra BV` or issuer.organization:`eMudhra Inc`)

The results list each certificate with its issuer, validity dates, and the assets and ports where it was found. Use the left-pane filters, such as Expiring Certificates and Certificate Authority, to sort the results by urgency.

The two organizations that matter most for this incident are eMudhra BV and eMudhra Inc, because they are the organizations named on the eight compromised intermediates (the G3B and G3C certificates).

Tip: save the query as a dashboard widget in Certificate View, so any new eMudhra-issued certificate that appears is flagged automatically.

Note: QQL query tokens are case-sensitive. If a query returns a syntax error, check the search token list in the Certificate View help and adjust the token name.

Response and Remediation

  1. Replace affected certificates first. Any leaf certificate whose chain includes one of the eight intermediates should be reissued by another trusted CA and redeployed with the correct chain.
  2. Updates. Apply operating system security updates and upgrade Go runtimes to supported releases that reject certificate chains containing the compromised intermediates.
  3. Confirm revocation behavior. eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates, but clients that do not check revocation can still accept them. Validate that certificate revocation checks are functioning correctly and that revocation lists are up to date.
  4. Monitor continuously. Monitor dashboards after each scan cycle until results are clean.

Conclusion

The eMudhra incident is a reminder that trust depends on both the certificates you present and the authorities you trust. Certificate View gives you the issuer search and dashboards to find eMudhra-issued certificates, and VMDR and Cloud Agent inventory show which hosts and applications still need vendor updates. Qualys enables organizations to quickly discover affected assets, validate exposure, and confidently prioritize response efforts.

Start your risk-free trial of VMDR. If you are not yet using VMDR to measure, communicate, and eliminate risk, start a 30-day trial and use Certificate View to get a full view of your certificates.

Start Your Trial

item.title: (Reliable)? php2shell exploitability, (Fri, Oct 23rd)
item.description: Yesterday everyone was running around like crazy (me included :) because of the php2shell vulnerability.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday everyone was running around like crazy (me included :) because of the php2shell vulnerability.

However, after looking closely at some published PoC's - and there is an unbelievable amount of AI generated - erm, slop - it looks like building a universal, reliable, one click exploit is quite difficult (unless I'm missing something, so please do let me know).

The PoC's that have been released so far have several pre-requirements and are almost cheating.

First, in order to have a clean initial state, the one PoC that makes sense sends a POST HTTP request with a number of small fields (3000 bytes each, 1001 of them), for bulk allocation pressure, prepare PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and then append a big field of 12 MB.
This guarantees that emalloc fails, since the PoC require that memory limit is set to 8 MB.

This is the first issue; in real world setups memory_limit is usually 128 MB, making this a bit more demanding.
An even bigger issue is that real world setups will have multiple workers - the demo uses a single-worker prefork configuration which guarantees that the next phase lands with this worker. In real world this is not guaranteed and an attacker would have to consume all workers and release one (and catch that one). Not sure how difficult this is.

The next phase now (phase 1) leaks the Zend MM chunk base, which is a piece of heap, from which the 2 MB-aligned Zend MM chunk base is extracted.
This is needed for calculation of HashTable.

Then phase 2 leaks the libphp.so base address.
This is needed to defeat ASLR, but it's not the only component required. Specifically, once Apache starts, it will pick a randomized base address for libphp.so. However, offsets of other functions/pointers in libphp.so will be static.

So phase 2 will leak one specific code pointer: zval_ptr_dtor, which has a static offset from libphp.so base address. In other words, by knowing this offset, we can calculate the base address of libphp.so and defeat ASLR.
The problem here is that this depends on many factors - how libphp.so was compiled, what's the exact PHP version, distro etc).
This is where shown PoC's are "cheating" they read offsets of zval_ptr_dtor (and zif_system) from libphp.so on the server.
In real world an attacker would have to know this. I presume someone could compile list of all possible options for commonly used distro combinations.

Now in phase 3 (and I haven't thoroughly checked this one), the exploit will change pDestructor to zif_system, and this will result in execution of code. There is one limit here; the size of command can be up to 14 bytes.

As we can see, there's a lot of prerequisites here that make a reliable exploit difficult.
I'm pretty sure that smart researchers that found the vulnerability know (much) more, but clearly it's not as simple as perhaps initially thought.

The general recommendation to put session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 should help, especially since there apparently is a way to bypass even the (currently) available fix so do put this until the next update.

--
Bojan
@bojanz / bojanz
INFIGO IS

(c) SANS Internet Storm Center. https://isc.sans.edu Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial 3.0 United States License.

item.title: Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks
item.description:
Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzes the LiteLLM 1.107.0 compromise, including Python startup hooks, credential theft, remote code loading, detections, and mitigations.

The post Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.
item.content:encoded:
1. Attack overview
  2. Technical details
  3. Mitigation and protection guidance
  4. Indicators of compromise
  5. References
  6. Learn More

On October 21, 2026, a compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release was published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) and distributed through official container images. The malicious package added files that Python could execute during normal interpreter initialization. An application did not need to import LiteLLM for the payload to run: starting Python in an affected environment could be enough.

Microsoft analyzed two execution paths in the affected wheels: a credential collector launched through a path extension, and a Unix-oriented loader persisted through site-specific configuration. The collector targeted authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. A separate database module attempted to read selected credential and model-configuration records from the LiteLLM proxy.

Endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the recovered collector’s discovery, encryption, and outbound-connection behavior. In one Windows example, a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated the collector. This distinction matters for response: investigators should not start Python or pip inside a suspect environment to determine whether the malicious package is present.

This blog explains the startup mechanisms, the credentials the payload could reach, and the evidence defenders can use to investigate exposure. It also provides Microsoft Defender detection information, advanced hunting queries, and recovery guidance. Removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery. Organizations must address the affected Python environment, any surviving processes, and credentials accessible to the compromised identity.

Attack overview

LiteLLM is commonly deployed as a gateway between applications and model providers. In that position it may have access to model-provider API keys, database connection strings, workload identities, routing configuration, and tenant policy data. The same package is also used on developer workstations, build agents, test systems, and containers, which widened the set of environments that could be exposed by the compromised release.

According to LiteLLM maintainers, stolen developer GitHub credentials were used to alter the release workflow and redirect it to the lookalike repository Berri-AI/litellm rather than the legitimate BerriAI/litellm repository. A credential associated with another developer account was then used to satisfy a production approval step. Microsoft has not independently determined how the attacker first accessed the upstream environment or obtained those credentials.

The compromised package used Python startup mechanisms to execute malicious code automatically, meaning exposure was not limited to systems actively using a LiteLLM gateway. Developer workstations, continuous integration and continuous delivery/deployment (CI/CD) agents, test environments, containers, and other systems that started Python with the affected package installed could also execute the payload. The malicious code supported credential collection and, on Unix-based systems, retrieval and execution of additional Python code.

1. Compromised package distribution

The compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release delivered malicious Python startup files to environments where the package was installed.

2. Automatic payload execution

Python startup processing launched the credential collector without requiring the application to actively use LiteLLM gateway functionality.

3. Credential and sensitive-data collection

The collector targeted developer credentials, cloud credentials, browser data, SSH material, environment variables, and LiteLLM database data accessible to the affected process.

4. Encryption and exfiltration

Collected data was encrypted and transmitted to an attacker-controlled endpoint.

5. Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code

On Unix-based systems, the payload supported retrieving and executing additional Python code, although this activity was not confirmed.

Technical details

Compromised package distribution and automatic payload execution

The compromised wheel packaged cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py under litellm-1.107.0.data/purelib/. During installation, these files were relocated into the Python environment’s library directory, outside the normal litellm application directory. This placement enabled execution through Python’s normal site initialization, which processes executable import statements in .pth files and later attempts to import the sitecustomize module.

The first execution path began with the single executable line in cook.pth: “import cook”. This loaded cook.py, whose wrapper Base64-decoded and zlib-decompressed an embedded Python program before executing the recovered source. The program identified itself as PRIVCOLLECT and performed credential collection in a daemon thread.

Before starting the thread, the collector checked the inherited PRIVCOLLECT_ACTIVE environment variable. A nonempty value caused it to return; otherwise, it set the flag, limiting duplicate collection in descendant processes. After an upload returned HTTP 200, it attempted to write /tmp/.pc_once_72129118c59f5636c0bb. These duplicate-suppression gates were not containment controls: startup alone did not prove collection or upload completed, because a short-lived process could exit before the thread finished, while write failures or temporary-storage changes could leave the marker absent.

A second startup mechanism used sitecustomize.py, providing a separate Unix-oriented execution path with an embedded collector and functionality to retrieve and execute additional Python code from a remote host. Remote retrieval and execution through this path were not confirmed.

Together, these mechanisms extended potential exposure beyond active LiteLLM deployments: simply starting Python in an affected environment could activate the malicious code, even when LiteLLM itself was never imported. Because the startup files resided outside the litellm application directory, removing only the application files could leave the malicious startup components behind.

Credential and sensitive-data collection

The recovered collector was designed to gather sensitive authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, browsers, and infrastructure. It runs multiple collection modules sequentially with independent error handling, allowing collection to continue even when individual targets are unavailable or inaccessible.

Encryption and exfiltration

After collection, the payload serializes module results and host metadata as JSON. Each run generates a 32-byte AES key and a 16-byte initialization vector. AES-256-CBC encrypts the collection document; an embedded 4,096-bit RSA public key wraps the AES key using OAEP. The OpenSSL path tries SHA-256 and then SHA-1 for OAEP, and the resulting metadata records the selected digest.

The collector places three members in a gzip-compressed tar archive: data.bin, containing the initialization vector (IV) and encrypted collection; key.bin, containing the wrapped AES key; and hdr.json, containing plaintext envelope metadata. It then attempts an HTTP POST to hxxp://www[.]litellm[.]dev/healthcheck, using application/octet-stream, a fixed browser-like User-Agent, and a body checksum in an X-SHA256 header. The upload routine retries and treats only HTTP 200 as success.

The OpenSSL backend creates temporary directories beginning with .pc_e_, stages input and output files and removes them after use.

Conditional retrieval and execution of additional code

In addition to the credential collector, the compromised package contained a separate Unix-oriented loader in sitecustomize.py, designed to retrieve and execute additional Python code. When Python starts, the loader takes an exclusive lock on /tmp/remote_code_loader.lock so that only one instance runs per host and detaches into the background. Each cycle reads a GitHub-hosted domain.txt file, which acts as a mutable pointer to an attacker-controlled server.

If a valid server address is returned and successfully resolved, the loader is designed to request /codepy from that server, compile the returned content, and execute it as Python code within the affected environment. This gives the attacker a mechanism to change the second-stage payload without publishing another compromised LiteLLM package. This loader is separate from the credential collector delivered directly in the compromised package.

At the time the cited researchers examined domain.txt, it was empty and no second-stage retrieval or execution was confirmed. Because the file could be changed, the loader remained a re-armable remote-code execution mechanism.

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following actions for organizations that installed, mirrored, or built images with LiteLLM 1.107.0:

  • Find and contain every affected copy. Identify LiteLLM 1.107.0 across installed environments, uv and pip caches, internal package mirrors, lock files, build outputs, and container images. Scope mutable container tags and the relevant exposure windows once validated and compare artifacts with the customer-ready hashes in the indicators of compromise section. For background, see secure software supply chain practices and Docker image digests. Digests are preferable to mutable tags because they identify immutable image content.
  • Prevent Python execution and investigate from outside the environment. Isolate affected developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts. Where operationally safe, stop running Python processes and prevent automation from restarting them. Do not run python, pip, or other commands that invoke the affected interpreter during evidence collection; inspect the environment with trusted tools from a known-clean system. Python normally processes site configuration, including executable import lines in .pth files, during initialization.
  • Rebuild from verified artifacts. Confirm that cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py were removed from the environment library path. Rebuilding is more reliable than assuming that deleting the litellm directory cleaned the top-level startup files.
  • Rotate reachable credentials from a known-clean machine. Include model-provider keys, cloud and workload credentials, CI/CD secrets, source-control and registry tokens, SSH and GPG keys, AI coding-tool tokens, and browser sessions available to the affected identity. On proxy hosts, include stored provider credentials and DATABASE_URL. Revoke affected identity sessions rather than assuming password or key rotation immediately invalidates every active token or application session. See revoke user access in Microsoft Entra ID.
  • Correlate before declaring compromise. Combine file hashes, Python process ancestry, .pc_e_ cryptographic staging, network destination, workload identity, and subsequent cloud or identity use. Do not use package presence or a generic filename as the sole verdict.
  • Strengthen dependency controls. Use hash-pinned lock files, verify package and image provenance, use container digests instead of floating tags, and admit packages to internal mirrors only after review. See best practices for a secure software supply chain and dependency scanning in Azure DevOps.
  • Restrict outbound access. Developer workstations, build agents, test systems, containers, and AI gateway hosts should not have unrestricted outbound HTTP access unless required. Route outbound traffic through managed egress controls, deny unnecessary destinations, and allowlist required services. See control outbound internet access from Azure.
  • Enable Microsoft Defender for Endpoint protections. Onboard supported developer workstations, build agents, and AI gateway servers to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus real-time and cloud-delivered protection where supported. See configure always-on protection and configure cloud protection.

Microsoft Defender XDR detections

As of October 22, 2026, the following Microsoft Defender Antivirus signatures and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint alerts were available for activity associated with the compromised LiteLLM 1.107.0 release. Detection names and availability may change as protection is updated.

Threat intelligence reports

Microsoft customers can use the following reports in Microsoft products to get the most up-to-date information about the threat actor, malicious activity, and techniques discussed in this blog. This report provides intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments.

Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics

Inside the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply chain compromise: Credential theft through Python startup hooks

Advanced hunting

These queries support investigation of the stages discussed above. Select the appropriate lookback in Defender XDR and correlate results with environment, process and identity evidence. They are investigation leads, not standalone verdicts.

Connections to the collector domain

Normalize URL/hostname observations before matching the campaign domain. The query rejects suffix lookalikes such as www[.]litellm[.]dev[.]example; a match still needs process and workload context.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| extend UrlForParsing = iff(RemoteUrl contains "://",
    RemoteUrl, strcat("http://", RemoteUrl))
| extend RemoteHost = trim_end(@"\.",
    tolower(tostring(parse_url(UrlForParsing).Host)))
| where RemoteHost in ("www.litellm.dev", "litellm.dev")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType,
    RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, ReportId

Known startup-file hashes

The four hashes cover LF and CRLF variants. A missing SHA-256 field limits this hunt; a generic filename is not an equivalent match.

DeviceFileEvents
| where SHA256 in~ (
    "9dd0a3926f96a37eb86cf1ee2310d9be93139cc4ebef3ef9e2efe9531390be25",
    "03ac2a8b752605d1d7710979c17ff18b03dd978203ba23ba97fd8ce3d6f897ea",
    "34bef04fe88ac9d0aae0475630b1738681d15b94f233ac8aa46eacf5968305fa",
    "b6122440d0d9cb1eb1ade9933f49214da8c31288de7710c076c2680dfa528465",
    "7f191632e7320705d154b85204f1ae546b543acbd7e8861229b76f5042b92bdb",
    "84dc8c82c0a4a4a62552ef826b49fcc86d1a5c4a5d0f2c06665723f93d129d7d")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ActionType,
    FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, ReportId

Inline database-collection program

Look for the sensitive table/field pair together with the query API, serialization and complete output-suppression pattern. Legitimate exports may overlap. The recovered parent’s /proc prerequisite limits its applicability; raw arguments are omitted because they can contain a database secret.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName startswith "python" or FileName startswith "platform-python"
| where strlen(ProcessCommandLine) <= 4096
| where ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "-c "
| where (ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "LiteLLM_CredentialsTable"
        and ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "credential_values")
    or (ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "LiteLLM_ProxyModelTable"
        and ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "litellm_params")
| where ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "query_raw"
| where ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "json.dumps("
    or ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "json.dump("
| where ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "os.devnull"
    and ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "os.dup2"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName,
    ProcessId, ProcessCreationTime, InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, ReportId

Collector-like encryption staging

The staging prefix plus encryption operation identifies a behavioral lead, not an upload or a uniquely malicious OpenSSL invocation. Alternate backends are outside this query, and key-bearing arguments are not projected.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName in~ ("openssl", "openssl.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine contains_cs ".pc_e_"
| where (ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " enc "
        and ProcessCommandLine contains_cs "-aes-256-cbc")
    or ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " pkeyutl "
    or ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " rsautl "
| extend CryptoOperation = iff(
    ProcessCommandLine contains_cs " enc ", "AES packaging", "RSA wrapping")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, CryptoOperation,
    ProcessId, ProcessCreationTime, InitiatingProcessFileName,
    InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCreationTime, ReportId

Vulnerability/Posture Check | Is the device potentially exposed to the affected Litellm?

Use this query to identify devices potentially exposed to TVM-2026-0003. A match indicates potential exposure, not confirmed exploitation or compromise.

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "TVM-2026-0003"

CloudProcessEvents query to detect encryption before exfiltration

Identifies OpenSSL public-key encryption using /tmp/.pc_ staging paths, consistent with key wrapping before potential exfiltration.

CloudProcessEvents
| where ProcessName == 'openssl' and ProcessCurrentWorkingDirectory has_any ('/runner/','/app','/tmp/')
    and ProcessCommandLine has_all ('pkeyutl','-encrypt','-pubin') and ProcessCommandLine contains '/tmp/.pc_'

MITRE ATT&CK techniques observed

Microsoft mapped the following techniques based on observed activity and analysis of the recovered malicious components; individual entries note where behavior was not confirmed. For standard industry documentation, refer to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.

Initial Access

  • T1195.001 Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools | Malicious files shipped in LiteLLM 1.107.0 wheels and images; upstream release abuse reported by the maintainer.

Persistence

  • T1546.018 Event Triggered Execution: Python Startup Hooks | cook.pth and sitecustomize.py run during Python site initialization.

Execution

  • T1059.006 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python | The collector runs in the interpreter; an inline Python child performs database queries.

Defense Evasion

  • T1027.013 Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File | Collector source is embedded as Base64-encoded, zlib-compressed content.
  • T1140 Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information | cook.py decodes and decompresses the collector at runtime.

Credential Access

  • T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files | Reads authentication and configuration files for developer, AI, and cloud tools.
  • T1552.004 Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys | Reads selected SSH, GPG, and TLS key material.
  • T1552.005 Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API | Requests AWS and GCP credentials from metadata services; returned credentials were not confirmed in Microsoft telemetry.
  • T1555.003 Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers | Copies browser databases and supports selected Chromium password recovery on Windows.

Discovery

  • T1082 System Information Discovery | systeminfo was launched by Python in an observed Windows sequence.
  • T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery | ipconfig, route, arp, and netstat were launched by the same Python process.

Collection

  • T1005 Data from Local System | Collects selected local histories, environment variables, and configuration.

Command and Control

  • T1102.001 Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver | The loader reads its server address from a specific GitHub-hosted file.
  • T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer | The loader can retrieve Python code from /codepy; retrieval and execution were not confirmed.

Indicators of compromise

URLs are defanged. Use precise roles and context rather than blocking shared infrastructure indiscriminately.

References

  • LiteLLM, Contained: Oct 21, 2026 LiteLLM release v1.107.0 Compromised
  • Python Software Foundation, Site-specific configuration hook.

Learn More

For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog.

To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky.

To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast.

Review our documentation to learn more about our real-time protection capabilities and see how to enable them within your organization.  

  • Learn more about securing Copilot Studio agents with Microsoft Defender 
  • Evaluate your AI readiness with our latest Zero Trust for AI workshop.
  • Microsoft 365 Copilot AI security documentation
  • How Microsoft discovers and mitigates evolving attacks against AI guardrails
  • Prompt injection protection in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 – official documentation of the prompt injection protection in Microsoft Defender for Office 365.

item.title: PHP Vulnerability Wrap-Up, (Fri, Oct 23rd)
item.description: This morning, we returned to Infocon Green. As usual, we are raising the Infocon to alert you to emerging situations requiring immediate attention. PHP fit that description. By now, you either know about it, or you probably never will, so it is time to go back to "business as usual".
item.content:encoded:
This morning, we returned to Infocon Green. As usual, we are raising the Infocon to alert you to emerging situations requiring immediate attention. PHP fit that description. By now, you either know about it, or you probably never will, so it is time to go back to "business as usual".

 Many vendors have released patches for the vulnerability in sync with PHP.net, showing that the coordinated vulnerability disclosure worked and achieved its goal of providing tested and working patches in a timely manner. Some vendor(s) not playing by the rules and leaking details early is unfortunate but should not overshadow the overall success of providing the patches.

At this point, no reliable exploit has been made available publicly as far as I know. Several firms stated that they possess working exploit code, and I consider it a matter of time before such code becomes publicly available, at which point we will likely see more widespread exploitation. Cloudflare and Amazon have stated that they are seeing a large number of exploit attempts, but it is not clear if these are actual working exploits.

Applying the patch remains your best and only reliable defense. Treat the time you have now as a gift and use it wisely to find and patch applications in your organization.

If you are not able to upgrade, do your best to isolate vulnerable applications. There are various workarounds, but none are considered 100% effective. They may buy you more time. The same is true for web application firewall rules.

Today, php.net advised keeping the "session.upload_progress.enabled=0" workaround in place until the next update. In other words: We are not done patching PHP yet!

As so often, embedded devices and appliances are a major concern, and many of them have not been updated or are unlikely to ever receive a patch. These types of devices should be isolated regardless. The PHP issue is likely just one of many weaknesses that could be exploited. Router admin interfaces, network storage devices, cameras, cat feeding stations, and refrigerators should not be exposed to the internet, and should be isolated on internal networks. At this point, this is table stakes regardless if they are running PHP.

This vulnerability is also a good "dress rehearsal" of what is likely going to come. Vulnerability disclosure worked in this case. Patches were available. There will likely be many more vulnerabilities of similar severity that will be released and exploited with less responsibility. Be ready, run your tabletop exercises, update your inventories... 

Many partial exploits have been released. Be careful; some of them may be "parasitic," trying to exploit whoever runs them. It may be hard to even identify the working exploit once it comes out.

The vulnerability and the risk are real, even if we did not see immediate mass exploitation. That part is still to come; it is just delayed. Just like we lower our infocon, make sure to rest and disconnect a bit, and do not stay "on alert" for too long. You will need the strength for the next issue. And do not overlook other issues that may have been missed this week: Node.js, Fortinet ... and more

--
Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu
Twitter|
