item.content:encoded:
Executive Summary

PHP2Shell is two critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS v4.0 9.2) that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on PHP installations serving web requests. Researchers have also demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of PHP worker memory, which can expose passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys. Cloudflare has already reported attack traffic, including attempts to evade its protections. Updating is the only complete fix: prioritize internet-facing deployments, starting with Apache mod_php, and assign an owner and remediation deadline to every system awaiting an update. This blog covers the fixed versions, PHP’s temporary mitigations, and how Qualys helps you discover exposure, mitigate risk before you can patch, and validate remediation.

What’s at Risk

PHP has released security updates for two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. Apache mod_php deployments warrant immediate attention: PHP reports a demonstrated exploit that can trigger before application code runs.

The vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, each carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2. Cloudflare has already reported attack traffic targeting these vulnerabilities, including attempts to evade its protections.

PHP identifies installations serving web requests as at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. Exploitability varies by configuration and application behavior.

Missed the PHP2Shell Emergency Briefing? Watch the on-demand briefing and demo to see how Qualys customers can quickly mitigate this threat.

Watch On-Demand Briefing

Not a Qualys customer? Access Qualys’ free PHP2Shell mitigation service to help protect your environment against this threat.

Sign Up for Free Mitigation Service

The Two Vulnerabilities

Both flaws involve PHP’s handling of memory and internal request state.

  • CVE-2026-109618 — Out-of-memory corruption: When an out-of-memory error interrupts a vulnerable operation, PHP leaves request data partially initialized. Cleanup routines then process that invalid state, creating a path to remote code execution.
  • CVE-2026-109619 — Stale global state: PHP retains references to request data after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker accesses those stale references before initialization resets them, triggering a use-after-free. Researchers have demonstrated remote code execution through this sequence.

Affected Deployments

While Apache mod_php is the most urgent priority, it is not the only deployment at risk. PHP-FPM also requires patching. Its startup behavior blocks a specific out-of-memory attack path, but PHP has validated session-lifecycle remote code execution against FPM under suitable application conditions.

Beyond code execution, researchers have also demonstrated unauthenticated disclosure of PHP worker memory. Exposed memory can contain passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys.

For root causes, CVSS vectors, and CWEs, see the Technical Appendix. Updating is the only complete fix, so the next step is to identify the fixed release for each PHP branch you run.

PHP2Shell by the Numbers: Nearly All PHP Installations Are Exposed

The Qualys Threat Research Unit analyzed anonymized data from more than 10,000 customers to measure exposure to PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The results show how large the problem is.

We found 167 million PHP package installations, of which 156M have a known PHP version and 73% of them are on internet-facing assets. That puts them within reach of remote attackers.

Among the 156 million installations with a known PHP version:

  • 44 million (28%) run supported branches, PHP 8.2 to 8.5. A fix is available for these versions, but it has not been applied yet.
  • 110 million (71%) run end-of-life or end-of-support versions of PHP, from 5.4 to 8.1. Most of these will never get a vendor patch, so upgrading to a supported branch is the only remedy.
  • Only 199,000 were patched in the first 12 hours after disclosure.

The takeaway: Nearly all PHP installations are either vulnerable or running unsupported versions.

Fixed Versions and Upgrade Guidance

The following upstream releases address both vulnerabilities:

For distribution-managed installations, use your vendor’s advisory to identify the fixed package. Backported fixes may retain an older upstream version number. 

PHP 8.1 and earlier remain outside regular upstream support. PHP has provided limited source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running those branches should obtain a fixed build from their distribution or support vendor, apply the appropriate source backport, or upgrade to a supported release.

When a fixed release cannot be deployed immediately, PHP recommends temporary measures to reduce exposure (see Temporary Mitigations Recommended by PHP in the Technical Appendix), and Qualys mitigation described below can also help. If a patched build cannot be deployed promptly, consider restricting public access or temporarily isolating the affected service while remediation is arranged. Patching, mitigating, and verifying all start with knowing where PHP runs in your environment.

How Qualys Can Help

Qualys helps you respond to PHP2Shell in three stages: discover and assess exposure, mitigate before you can patch, and remediate and validate.

1. Discover and Assess Exposure

The first step is knowing where PHP runs and which installations are vulnerable.

Inventory PHP Installations

Qualys customers can begin discovery with QID 45110 – PHP Server Detected, an Information Gathered (IG) check.

QID 45110 identifies PHP installations; it does not confirm vulnerability to either CVE. Use its results to identify systems for review, then validate each installation against the applicable PHP or vendor advisory.

Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) can help teams inventory PHP installations, identify end-of-life software, and prioritize internet-facing assets for remediation. It shows every asset where PHP is installed, so teams can scope PHP2Shell remediation in minutes.

Run the following queries in CSAM > Inventory > Assets.

All assets with PHP installed

(software: ((name: "php")))

Assets running end-of-life PHP (8.1 and earlier)

((software: (((name: "PHP") AND (version: (*..8.1))))))

PHP on your most critical assets

((asset.criticalityScore: [4..*)) AND (software: (((name: "PHP") AND (version: (*..8.1))))))

Use QID 45110 to establish your PHP discovery baseline, keep software inventory current, and configure InstaScan to cover the relevant assets. With the baseline in place, use the vulnerability detection QIDs below to assess PHP2Shell exposure and verify remediation.

Detection QIDs

Qualys released the following detection QIDs, which are now available. We will add distribution-specific detection QIDs to this blog as they are released.

As distributions publish their own advisories, InstaScan helps you act on them without waiting for the next scheduled scan.

Detect Exposure the Moment Distributions Release Their Patches

With Qualys InstaScan, powered by Agent Insta, new vendor advisories become actionable exposure findings using the software inventory your environment already reports. InstaScan continuously matches advisory intelligence against that inventory, surfacing findings for assets in scope, typically within minutes of advisory processing, without requiring a new scan. Your team can begin investigating and prioritizing remediation while the next scheduled scan is still hours away.

For PHP2Shell, this brings faster visibility as distribution-specific advisories become available. Supported advisory sources include Red Hat, Ubuntu, Debian, and Oracle Linux, helping teams respond across mixed Linux environments.

Package-level findings are only part of the picture, because PHP copies can also live outside standard locations.

How to Safely Validate the PHP2Shell Exploit Path on Internet-Facing Assets

Version matching identifies PHP hosts running unfixed releases, but not which are exploitable right now. Security teams need to know where the entry point is actually open. Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Management (ETM) uses TruConfirm to safely validate exploitability on live production assets without disruption.

How it works:

  1. Verify the target. Confirm the server runs PHP before proceeding.
  2. Send a benign probe. A carefully crafted upload request mimics the attacker’s initial move without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure.
  3. Confirm exposure. PHP startup warnings indicate the php2shell entry point is reachable and the recommended mitigation, session.upload_progress.enabled=0, is absent.

Confirmed exposures receive an amplified TruRisk score and move up the remediation queue with supporting evidence. ETM combines exploit validation with version-based detection to show both whether the entry point is exposed and whether the PHP build is patched. 

Lastly, remediate and verify. Upgrade PHP and restart all workers, or disable session upload progress if unused. Revalidate to confirm the entry point is no longer reachable and provide evidence for auditors. Safely validate the PHP2Shell exploit path across your internet-facing assets with TruConfirm in ETM today.

In a real customer environment, 1,539 assets were running PHP, but only 25 were confirmed to be exploitable. This highlights the power of TruConfirm, the AI-driven exploit validation in Qualys ETM. Instead of providing your team with a lengthy list of 1,539 assets to investigate, TruConfirm safely identifies which ones attackers can actually reach and exploit, all while operating on live production assets without creating files, executing code, or disrupting operations. By combining this validation with threat intelligence and asset context, TruConfirm helps your team move from detection to hyper-prioritization, so they can focus on the less than 2% of assets that matter most, backed by solid evidence for every decision.

A Caution Before You Test: Public PoCs Are Demonstrations, Not Validation Tools

 Since disclosure, PHP2Shell proof-of-concept scripts have spread quickly on GitHub. They are useful for understanding the research. However, they are not a safe way to check whether a production server is exposed, and running one against an internet-facing asset can cause exactly the kind of disruption you are trying to prevent. A PoC run against a live target typically does four things:

  • It ties up PHP workers. Some widely shared scripts hold a single upload open for close to a minute. Others send oversized requests to force an out-of-memory condition. Against a small worker pool or a busy server, either can leave legitimate requests waiting while the test runs.
  • It writes attacker-controlled data to disk. The technique records client-supplied upload data into a real session file on the server. In the public scripts that data carries PHP code. The demonstration payload is harmless on its own, but the staging mechanism is identical to what an attacker would use, and an interrupted run can leave that file behind.
  • It walks the vulnerable code path. PHP2Shell is a memory-corruption vulnerability. A PoC demonstrates exploitability by triggering that corruption directly. On an unpatched build, that is the same condition that can take down a worker. These scripts were tuned to the researcher’s lab, not to your build, your traffic, or your uptime requirements.
  • It may not be what it claims to be. High-profile vulnerabilities routinely attract look-alike exploit code. Treat any PoC as untrusted and check where it connects and what it writes, and never run it from a system with access to your environment.

PoCs have a place. Clone the asset into an isolated lab, snapshot it, and run them there. On production, validate without walking the vulnerable path at all. That is what the approach above is built for: TruConfirm confirms the entry point is reachable and that the recommended mitigation is absent, without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure. Keep in mind that to a WAF or SIEM, PoC traffic looks like an attack, and against systems you do not own it will be treated as one.

Find Vulnerable PHP Installations Beyond Standard Locations with Qualys Deep Scan

Customers can use QID 389102 to assess PHP2Shell exposure. To broaden visibility into PHP installations outside standard locations, customers can also perform Qualys Deep Scan.

Deep Scan identifies vulnerable PHP binaries in custom application folders, secondary drives, and other configured directories. Findings appear in VMDR with the full binary path, installed version, and recommended fixed version, giving security and IT teams the details needed to locate and remediate overlooked installations.

This additional visibility matters when multiple PHP copies exist for the same asset: updating the primary installation can leave other copies vulnerable. Customers can tailor inspection through directory inclusion and exclusion rules, scan schedules, and resource controls. Deep Scan is included with VMDR and is available on Windows assets running Cloud Agent 6.2 or later. 

Identify Vulnerable PHP Across Cloud Images, Containers, and Serverless Workloads

PHP vulnerabilities can extend beyond traditional servers into cloud-native environments, including Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), container images, Kubernetes workloads, and serverless functions.

With Qualys TotalCloud and Container Security, organizations can identify vulnerable PHP components across AMIs, container registries, build artifacts, and deployed workloads. Qualys correlates container images with running containers, serverless and Kubernetes workloads, helping teams identify which vulnerable images are actively deployed in production rather than simply stored in a registry.

Go beyond package presence with Runtime Vulnerability Reachability. Using its eBPF-based Container Runtime Sensor, Qualys identifies vulnerable software packages observed in use within running containers and correlates this runtime evidence with vulnerability findings. Combined with internet exposure and workload context, this helps security teams prioritize PHP vulnerabilities affecting actively running applications.

This enables organizations to trace affected workloads back to their container images, update vulnerable dependencies, rebuild images, and redeploy patched workloads.

Respond to PHP2Shell Exposure Across Web Applications and APIs

PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) affects the underlying PHP runtime. Web applications and APIs running on vulnerable PHP versions may be at risk of remote code execution.

Identifying vulnerable hosts is only part of the challenge. Security teams also need to determine which applications are internet-facing, where potential exposure exists, and which affected systems require immediate remediation.

Qualys TotalAppSec connects application-level exposure with infrastructure-level vulnerability intelligence, extending PHP exposure visibility beyond host-based detection to the web applications and APIs that attackers can reach.

Qualys answers three operational questions:

Through application discovery and the identification of exposed PHP version information, TotalAppSec flags potentially affected applications, including those whose underlying runtimes may not be fully represented in host inventories. While exposed version information provides a useful indicator, confirming vulnerability requires validating the actual PHP runtime version and patch status.

By combining TotalAppSec’s application-level visibility with vulnerability findings from Qualys VMDR and TotalCloud, security teams can identify internet-facing applications that are affected by affected PHP runtimes and prioritize remediation based on exposure and risk.

Following remediation, teams can rescan applications with TotalAppSec to reassess externally visible PHP version information, while using VMDR and TotalCloud assessments to verify that the underlying PHP runtimes have been patched. This combined approach helps organizations move from identifying potential PHP2Shell exposure to prioritizing remediation and validating that affected workloads have been secured.

Customers can use the following QIDs to detect PHP2Shell exposure in web applications and APIs:

Fight Back Against PHP2Shell with Qualys

Our new PHP2Shell “Fightback” dashboard gives you one place to find every PHP instance in your environment, see which ones are actually at risk, and decide what to fix first.

Know Your Full PHP Footprint

  • Every asset running PHP software, with detections from the past week
  • Source-based discovery, so you can see how each instance was found
  • Safe instances separated out, so you can focus on what needs attention

See Where the Real Risk Is

  • Internet-facing instances and attack surface exposure
  • End-of-life and unpatched PHP versions, with EOL/EOS breakouts
  • Apache HTTP Server mod_php risk
  • General web service and header exposures

Prioritize and Act Fast

  • PHP2Shell prioritization, with high-risk assets grouped by OS
  • InstaScan detections of PHP2Shell in under a day
  • Detection age and current state (active, fixed, reopened) to track remediation progress

As new CVEs and patches roll out for each PHP version, we’ll keep tuning and updating the dashboard.

Download the PHP2Shell Fightback Dashboard today.

Download Now

2. Mitigate Before You Can Patch

Qualys Mitigation available for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619

This mitigation follows PHP’s mitigation guidance, with additional insights from the Qualys Threat Research Unit (TRU).

This mitigation disables the PHP session upload-progress feature across every web-facing PHP runtime on the  host and hardens the related session-handling configuration. This removes the vulnerable code path from execution without changing the application itself.

It is a configuration-level change applied to each affected PHP interpreter, and the  PHP service must be restarted for  it to take effect. The mitigation restarts the service automatically; if the logs show a restart is still required, you can restart the PHP service manually. After the restart, the effective configuration is verified to confirm the setting is active and not overridden elsewhere.

This is an interim risk-reduction measure that eliminates the flaw’s reachability.

Mitigation Details via Qualys Dashboards 

Qualys mitigations have been available for more than 12 hours. Customers with vulnerable detections can see the following mitigation options on their dashboards.

Select the “Mitigate Now” option on this familiar screen.

Mitigation reduces risk in the interim, but updating remains the only complete fix. The final step is confirming that every fix has taken effect.

Mitigate PHP Servers Without an Agent

PHP2Shell hits hardest where you have the least reach. Of the 167M PHP installations Qualys found, 156M had a known PHP version, of which 73% are internet-facing and 110M (71%) run end-of-life or end-of-support branches outside upstream support. Many internet-facing PHP servers sit on appliances, DMZ servers, legacy hosts, and systems owned by other teams. These are often the hardest systems to reach, and many can’t run a Cloud Agent.

A network scan can show that these systems are exposed, but mitigating them has usually meant someone logging in and changing configurations by hand, one server at a time. With unauthenticated remote code execution on the table, that pace leaves your perimeter open.

The mitigation script for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 is now available in through the Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) library in TruRisk Eliminate, and you can run it directly on scanner-based hosts. The same platform that finds the exposure can now mitigate it, without deploying an agent first.

  • Find your scanner-only hosts. Identify exposed PHP servers with QID 389102 and the unauthenticated check, QID 39033, starting with your external perimeter.
  • Run the mitigation with TruRisk Eliminate. Select the PHP2Shell mitigation script in the CAR library and run it on your scanner-based hosts.
  • Confirm the mitigation. 

Patch With Confidence

PHP has released upstream fixes, but many vendor and distribution patches are still rolling out. Until a patch is available for your environment, mitigations remain the priority.

Where vendor patches are available, you can deploy them within TruRisk Eliminate. Right now, that includes Ubuntu’s PHP security updates. 

For the Ubuntu patch:

  • Patch reliability: High. Qualys rates these updates with a High patch reliability score, which means they’re unlikely to disrupt production.
  • No OS reboot required. USN-8948-1 updates only PHP userspace packages (php8.1, php8.3, php8.5), not the kernel or core system libraries.
  • Restart every service that loads PHP. Running processes keep the vulnerable code in memory until they restart. This matters especially for CVE-2026-109619, which exploits request state that carries over when PHP workers are reused.

3. Remediate and Verify

After remediation, rerun the applicable checks and verify that both the installed packages and running PHP instances include the fixes.

By combining web application and API security findings with PHP vulnerability detections from VMDR and TotalCloud, security teams can better prioritize remediation of internet-facing applications backed by vulnerable PHP installations. After patching the underlying PHP runtime, teams should rescan affected assets and applications to validate remediation.

For a step-by-step verification checklist, see Confirm That Remediation Is Complete in the Technical Appendix.

New to Qualys and want to find out your exposure to PHP2Shell?

Sign up for Free Mitigation Service

Technical Appendix for Security Teams

Current Vulnerability Information for Both CVEs

CWEs (both CVEs): CWE-416 Use After Free; CWE-755 Improper Handling of Exceptional Conditions; CWE-824 Access of Uninitialized Pointer; CWE-1325 Improperly Controlled Sequential Memory Allocation; CWE-1419 Incorrect Initialization of Resource.

Based on the PHP-assigned CVSS scores, exploitation requires no privileges or user interaction and results in a full impact. However, both Attack Complexity (AC:H) and Attack Requirements (AT:P) are set because exploitation depends on the allocator layout, build, and worker scheduling.

Temporary Mitigations Recommended by PHP

Updating is the only complete fix. The following measures, drawn from PHP’s release announcement and detailed security advisories, reduce exposure to specific attack paths. They do not make an unpatched installation safe.

Technical Details

If you cannot update today, PHP recommends a few configuration changes that help reduce the risk to affected assets. The table below explains the reason behind each change.

The guidance below expands on each of these settings by CVE.

CVE-2026-109618: Out-of-Memory Corruption

  • Enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through php_admin_value in the FPM pool or Apache configuration. Restart every PHP worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit. This removes the attacker-controllable failure caused by PHP’s configured memory limit. Underlying allocation failures can still reach the vulnerable code.
  • Set conservative request limits. Use post_max_size=8M for applications that do not require file uploads, or post_max_size=32M where uploads are necessary. Keep upload_max_filesize below post_max_size.
  • Limit request size and complexity. Independently enforce decoded request-size limits at the web server or proxy, including requests without a usable Content-Length. Reduce max_input_nesting_level and bound input variables, multipart parts, headers within each part, and uploads. Consider enforcing these additional limits at the web server or proxy. If the application does not use multipart form data, block those requests before they reach PHP.
  • Use container or cgroup memory limits as an availability boundary, preferably configured to terminate only the affected worker. These limits do not guarantee protection against allocation failures. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can force allocation failures that trigger the vulnerable path.

Note: Setting memory_limit=-1 removes PHP’s per-request memory cap and increases the risk of resource exhaustion. Treat it as a temporary measure and account for available resources and worker-level limits.

CVE-2026-109619: Stale Global State

  • Set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 before request parsing, using php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration, and restart every worker. Do not rely on application-level ini_set() or FPM .user.ini. This blocks the confirmed session paths only.
  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This blocks the confirmed fatal-backtrace path only.
  • Remove invalid or deprecated per-request settings that generate diagnostics before initialization. Also resolve warnings and other diagnostics produced during extension post-deactivation or server cleanup. Suppressing messages through error_reporting, display_errors, or @ does not prevent the underlying access.
  • Fix fatal errors and execution timeouts that attackers can trigger, including failures in callbacks, uploads, imports, and cleanup. Address the underlying failure; changing timeout settings alone does not cover other vulnerable paths.
  • For PHP-FPM, consider pm.max_requests=1 if the performance cost is acceptable. This limits each worker to one request. It is an optional measure for FPM and does not replace patching.

If a patched build cannot be deployed promptly, consider restricting public access or temporarily isolating the affected service while remediation is arranged. Assign an owner and a remediation deadline to each system awaiting an update.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

Installing a package is one step. Verify that each application is actually using the patched runtime.

  1. Find every PHP installation. Include parallel PHP branches, containers, hosting-panel packages, and PHP bundled with appliances or other software. The version returned by php -v may belong to a different installation from the one serving web requests.
  2. Update the correct package, binary, or image. For distribution packages, check the complete package version against the vendor’s advisory. For container deployments, obtain a patched image or rebuild your application image with patched dependencies.
  3. Restart or replace affected workers. Restart the relevant services or redeploy containers, then confirm that the running application uses the updated runtime. Check for workers that remain on the previous build.
  4. Review emergency configuration changes. After verifying the patched runtime, restore an appropriate finite memory_limit and review temporary upload restrictions and worker-recycling settings. Test application behavior under memory pressure: the patched runtime can terminate a worker immediately at its hard memory threshold, bypassing normal shutdown handlers.
  5. Verify Web Applications and APIs. After patching the affected PHP runtimes and restarting the associated services, rescan your web applications and APIs using Qualys TotalAppSec with QIDs 533086 and 533068, as needed, to reassess exposure to PHP2Shell and validate the effectiveness of your remediation efforts.

    Important: Exercise caution when using QID 533068. This QID performs an intrusive vulnerability check that may cause unpatched PHP applications or APIs to crash, potentially disrupting service availability. We recommend enabling this check only in non-production environments or on systems that have been confirmed to be patched. Before running QID 533068 in production, evaluate the potential operational impact, obtain the necessary approvals, and conduct testing within an approved maintenance window. Avoid running this check against unpatched or unverified production systems.  

    For complete remediation verification, also check the installed PHP version and patch status using Qualys VMDR or TotalCloud assessments.

Connect Your AI Assistant to Qualys in Three Steps

You can now bring Qualys data into your AI workflows with qualys-cli-mcp, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for the Qualys Cloud Platform. Claude, Cursor, VS Code, and other MCP-capable assistants can use it to query your Qualys environment in plain language. For example, you can ask “Can you check in Qualys if I’m vulnerable to CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619″ without writing API calls or switching consoles.

That’s it. Your assistant can now work across Qualys.

Reference

PHP Security Team – Upcoming Critical PHP Security Release

item.title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
item.description: Following the discovery that eight eMudhra intermediate certificates use weak keys, Cloudflare is deploying mitigations and releasing client updates. We explain the impact, our response, and what customers and developers should do next.
item.content:encoded:
On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.

We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.

We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.

Our response

We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms.

Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below.

What customers should do

Developer guidance

For developers, look beneath the SDK.

An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.

Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.

This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.

Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.

Timeline

The timeline of events so far is below.

Date and Time

Event

October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC

Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment.

October 20, 02:00 UTC

Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms.

October 20 09:15 UTC

Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published.

October 20 19:20 UTC

CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed.

Looking forward

The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just one application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.

item.title: The Real Jump Scare Isn’t the Attacker; It’s The Vulnerabilities You’re Focusing On
item.description: Key Takeaways Teams are remediating more than ever, but exposure from the vulnerabilities that matter is still rising faster than they can keep up with. Mean time to exploitation is about −7 days. Mean time to remediate sits around +30 days. Qualys research: closures rose from 73M (2022) to 473M (2025) – 6× – while […]
item.content:encoded:
Key Takeaways

  • Teams are remediating more than ever, but exposure from the vulnerabilities that matter is still rising faster than they can keep up with.
  • Mean time to exploitation is about −7 days. Mean time to remediate sits around +30 days.
  • Qualys research: closures rose from 73M (2022) to 473M (2025) – 6× – while critical findings still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%.
  • Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited. A volume-and-CVSS program spends most of its effort on the rest.
  • 15% of organizations that operationalized the pipeline patched before a vulnerability hit the CISA KEV list.

October is here, bringing a chill in the air, spooky decorations, and, fittingly, Cybersecurity Awareness Month. It’s a timely reminder for security leaders to revisit and strengthen their strategy. The past 12 months alone show how cyber threats are getting smarter and faster.

There’s a haunting paradox that should be top of mind. Security teams are doing more vulnerability remediation than ever before. They’re patching faster, scanning deeper, and closing more tickets than any team in history, yet attackers exploit systems at an alarming rate, faster than ever before.

Fortunately, with the right cyber risk management plan, security teams can navigate the dark landscape of AI-driven attackers. But before we talk about defense, let’s outline a few of attackers’ tricks.

The Threat Landscape Is Accelerating

Ransomware is one of the leading cyber threats, rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year, and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031. If that projection holds, it will put severe pressure on already strained security teams.

AI is escalating the problem rather than easing it. AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost. More attacks are coming, and those powered by AI make each breach more expensive to address.

The increased frequency and sophistication combined result in a spine-chilling number: mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days. Which means, on average, weaponization arrives a week before defenders have anything to deploy. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days. The attacker’s clock starts before defenders have anything to deploy, so the defenders are already behind before their own 30-day countdown even begins. And there’s a scary price attached.

The Financial Reality

Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead, turning every minute into a running invoice. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident, up 12% from last year.

The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average. The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average.

With costs escalating like this, the expectation would be that a growing volume of patching work is buying that cost down. The data says otherwise.

The Remediation Paradox

Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that while the effort to address vulnerabilities went up, exposure still rose alongside it. According to the research, effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. As a result, enterprises did far more work and ended up further behind. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%. More effort produced less coverage where it counted.

The reason traces back to how that effort gets allocated in the first place. Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited, which means a program built around volume and severity score spends the majority of its effort on vulnerabilities attackers were never going to use. The 6x increase didn’t close the gap since most of that work was never aimed at the 1% that mattered.

This misalignment proves detrimental for the vulnerabilities that do get weaponized. Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half were weaponized before a patch existed. Teams were doing the work. They just weren’t always working on the right thing, at the right time.

The light in the dark here is that there are organizations winning this race. 15% of organizations that operationalized their remediation pipeline patched before the vulnerability was even added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) list. This is proof that the gap isn’t fixed in place. It closes when the model changes.

As risk accelerates, the organizations that shift away from a ‘fix everything’ mindset to disciplined, continuous, business-impact-based prioritization will be prepared for the unknown. The focus should be on automated, intelligence-driven remediation that assesses risk in real time rather than adding people to a process.

The Path Forward

So what does this shift look like? It starts with context, not more volume. Remediation becomes contextual rather than sequential. Most friction between IT and security doesn’t start with the vulnerability itself. It starts when a ticket arrives without ownership data, gets validated whether or not action is warranted, and then gets reassigned before anything is fixed.

When asset context and risk intelligence route tasks before a ticket is even created, that upstream friction disappears. MTTR drops 30% and response times improve 40%. That’s what happens when decisions about what really matters get made before the backlog forms, instead of getting caught in debates once issues arise.

In a digital age where attacks are happening faster than teams can keep up, the teams still haunted by their own remediation metrics are the ones still asking the old questions: how many vulnerabilities can we close? What’s the CVSS score? How long before we remediate? The organizations that are getting safer are asking a different set of questions: Is this actively being exploited? What’s the evidence? Which assets are at risk? What can we automate?

As we recognize Cybersecurity Awareness Month, it’s crucial to remember that diligence is non-negotiable; the real key lies in prioritizing the vulnerabilities that wield the greatest impact.

Scary Stats That Will Keep You Up At Night

  • Ransomware is rising in both frequency and cost. It now factors into 48% of breaches, up from 44% from the previous year, and attacks are projected to occur every two seconds by 2031.
  • AI-generated attacks have increased 56% between March 2025 and February 2026, adding $1 million in cost per breach to the baseline cost.
  • Mean time to exploitation is now measured at -7 days. Mean time to remediate, by comparison, sits at +30 days.
  • Every hour a breach remains active costs organizations roughly $1,100 in operational disruption, lost productivity, and incident response overhead. Globally, a breach averages about $5 million per incident, up 12% from last year.
  • The U.S. is projected to have the highest breach cost at about $11.5 million – more than twice the global average.
    • The Middle East, Benelux, and Germany follow, with all four regions experiencing higher breach costs than the global average.
  • Research by the Qualys Threat Research Unit found that effort was allocated by volume and severity score instead of by evidence of what attackers were using. Closures rose from 73 million in 2022 to 473 million in 2025, a 6x increase in output, while the share of critical vulnerabilities still open at day seven rose from 56% to 63%.
  • Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited.
    • A program built around volume and severity score spends the majority of its effort on vulnerabilities attackers were never going to use.
  • Across the most critical, actively exploited vulnerabilities over the past four years, manual remediation processes failed to keep pace with attackers 88% of the time, and half were weaponized before a patch existed.

References

  1. Verizon. “2026 Data Breach Investigations Report.” July 29, 2026. https://www.verizon.com/business/resources/reports/dbir/?CMP=OOH_SMB_OTH_22222_MC_20200501_NA_NM20200079_00001#key-resources
  2. Astra. “State of continuous pentesting report 2026.” June 2026. https://www.getastra.com/reports/state-of-pentesting
  3. IBM. “Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026.” July 29, 2026. https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach?utm_medium=OSocial&utm_source=Youtube&utm_content=RSRWW&utm_id=YT-201-CODB-2026
  4. Mandiant. “M-Trends 2026 Report: Real-world investigations and actionable defense insights.” March 23, 2026. https://cloud.google.com/security/resources/m-trends
  5. Statista. “Average cost of a data breach worldwide from March 2024 to February 2026, by country or region.” July 2026. https://www.statista.com/statistics/463714/cost-data-breach-by-country-or-region/

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q: What is the remediation paradox?
A: Organizations are closing far more vulnerabilities, Qualys research shows a 6× rise in closures from 2022 to 2025, while a larger share of critical findings remain open at day seven. More effort has not produced better coverage of the exposures attackers use.

Q: What does mean time to exploitation of −7 days mean?
A: On average, weaponization arrives about a week before defenders have a deployable fix, so the defender’s clock starts already behind.

Q: Why not just fix everything?
A: Less than 1% of vulnerabilities are actively exploited. A program built on volume and CVSS spends most of its effort on findings attackers were never going to use.

Q: What should teams ask instead?
A: Is this actively exploited? What is the evidence? Which assets are at risk? What can be automated?

Q: Did any organizations beat the clock?
A: Yes. Qualys research found 15% of organizations that leveraged autonomous remediation patched before a vulnerability was added to the CISA KEV list.

item.title: The Risk of AI-Powered Antidetect Browsers in Online Fraud and Influence Operations
item.description:
Key Findings Introduction Antidetect browsers conceal their users’ digital identities, enabling a single operator or small team to simultaneously run thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Twitter/X, Discord, LinkedIn, Reddit, and many more, without triggering the detection systems employed by those platforms. In this report, we highlight three […]

The post The Risk of AI-Powered Antidetect Browsers in Online Fraud and Influence Operations appeared first on Check Point Research.
item.content:encoded:
Key Findings

  • Antidetect browsers obscure the digital identity of their users, enabling a single operator to silently manage thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms (including Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube), while evading detection systems that look for scams and coordinated inauthentic behavior.
  • Threat actors abuse these platforms, taking over accounts and using them for financial fraud, phishing and malware distribution. These accounts can also be used to coordinate influence operations, which becomes an even greater concern ahead of elections.
  • Social platforms primarily detect coordinated activity at the account and behavioral layer. Antidetect browsers run below the surface enabling them to remain undetected.
  • The three main antidetect browsers we discuss in this report are Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin.
  • These tools already use AI integration, from built-in automation templates to offering a dedicated MCP server that pipes LLM-generated content directly into pre-warmed account profiles at machine speed. Running a large-scale social media operation now requires only a credit card instead of a technical team.

Introduction

Antidetect browsers conceal their users’ digital identities, enabling a single operator or small team to simultaneously run thousands of isolated accounts across multiple platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Twitter/X, Discord, LinkedIn, Reddit, and many more, without triggering the detection systems employed by those platforms.

In this report, we highlight three main tools: Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin. We selected these specifically on the basis of documented references across underground forums and criminal marketplaces, indicating active adoption beyond their stated commercial purposes. Confirmed use cases include:

  • Account takeover operations in which session cookies harvested by infostealer malware are injected into clean browser profiles to assume control of banking accounts and cryptocurrency wallets without triggering authentication alerts.
  • Carding operations in which stolen payment credentials are tested across e-commerce platforms under the guise of distinct legitimate users.
  • Fraudulent loan applications submitted under fabricated identities.
  • Bulk creation of artificial accounts used to generate fraudulent advertising revenue at scale.

As documented in Anthropic’s September 2026 Threat Intelligence Report, attackers used antidetect browsers in a fraud campaign that targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and financial marketplaces. They combined antidetect browser profiles, residential proxies, automated CAPTCHA-solving, and identity-verification bypass tools to create large numbers of verified accounts while avoiding onboarding security checks. These accounts were later used in fraud operations.

The risk posed by antidetect browsers is greater because these accounts pass KYC verification, build legitimate activity histories, and appear benign during transactions. As a result, fraud detection systems that rely on user behavior or device identity often cannot identify these accounts as suspicious until after fraudulent activity has already occurred.

The antidetect browsers documented in this research are commercially available, legally registered platforms with documented legitimate use cases in digital marketing, e-commerce, and privacy protection. When deployed by threat actors, the same infrastructure that enables financial fraud at scale is equally applicable to Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior (CIB), the term used to describe organized manipulation campaigns in which false identities are central to the operation and adversarial methods are used to evade detection.

Meta’s most recent transparency reporting explicitly flagged this as a growing concern, with Russia, Iran, and China identified as the three leading sources of such activity globally.

The Identity Obfuscation Stack – How antidetect browsers defeat social media platform detection at every layer

Figure 1 – The five layers through which antidetect browsers defeat platform detection methods.

While antidetect browsers are not a new phenomenon, their threat potential has increased with the integration of AI. Previously, their operational impact was constrained by the manual effort required to run and maintain large account networks at scale. AI-assisted content generation, automated persona management, and machine-speed distribution pipelines now enables a single actor with a subscription and a prompt to do the work of a coordinated team.

In the following sections, we provide a technical breakdown of each tool, examining capabilities documented on their own platforms, underground forum references, and the specific features that position them as an emerging threat.

Figure 2 – Comparison of popular antidetect tools.

Defeating Platform Detection: The Identity Layer No Platform Can See

Companies like Meta, TikTok, and Google have spent billions of dollars building behavioral and identity detection systems to identify abuse of their platforms for scams, financial fraud, and coordinated inauthentic activity. Antidetect browsers are engineered to defeat every signal on which those systems rely.

Every antidetect browser uses fingerprint spoofing. When a browser connects to a website, it exposes dozens of identifying parameters that the website can collect to build a browser fingerprint, including canvas rendering output, WebGL vendor and renderer strings, font enumeration behavior, screen resolution, time zone, user agent, and hardware identifiers. Platforms cross-reference these signals to determine whether two accounts originate from the same device. Antidetect browsers intercept and fabricate each of these parameters individually, assigning a unique combination to every profile.

The criminal ecosystem surrounding these tools extends well beyond their commercial vendors. As seen in Figure 3, a threat actor on a Russian-language underground forum advertised an AiTM engine as a commercial service, with built-in functionality to export harvested session credentials directly into antidetect browsers. The post confirms that the pipeline from credential harvesting to antidetect-assisted account takeover is a documented, commercially available and actively traded workflow with dedicated tooling, published instructions, and an active buyer community.

Figure 3 – An AiTM engine advertised as a commercial service on a Russian-language underground forum, with built-in functionality to export harvested session credentials directly into antidetect browsers.

Kameleo

Modifying browser engines at the source level rather than applying surface overrides, Kameleo produces fingerprints drawn from real device signatures, making them significantly harder to flag as anomalous. Its adoption within criminal ecosystems is evidenced by its repeated appearance across the most active Russian-language hacking forums. As seen in Figure 4, Kameleo is listed alongside other antidetect browsers in a post by a proxy seller on an underground forum, advertising residential proxy services explicitly marketed for account farming, CAPTCHA bypass, and shield evasion against security systems including DataDome, the same platform for which Kameleo’s own blog publishes dedicated bypass guides.

Figure 4 – A proxy seller on an underground forum listing Kameleo as part of a complete operational stack. The service is explicitly marketed for account farming and bulk account management.

Kameleo’s engineering team published a guide detailing how to automate Facebook likes across multiple accounts simultaneously using precisely this fingerprint manipulation. As seen in Figure 5, evading platform detection is not a side effect but the tool’s primary operational value.

Figure 5 – Kameleo’s guide on how to automate Facebook likes across multiple accounts simultaneously using browser fingerprint manipulation.

Beyond fingerprinting, Kameleo suppresses WebRTC, a protocol that can leak a device’s real IP address even when a proxy is active, and provides explicit configuration options to prevent non-proxied UDP connections. The documentation frames this not as a privacy feature but as a counter to a known de-anonymization vector used by platform security teams.

At the session layer, Kameleo’s dedicated cookie injection API accepts complete cookie objects including session IDs, refresh tokens, and authentication flags, allowing a pre-authenticated session state to be inserted into a profile before it is launched. The platform sees the profile as an already-authenticated user, with no login event occurring to trigger anomaly detection. As independently documented by threat intelligence research and confirmed by security researchers, this workflow is established and active in the criminal ecosystem. Figure 6 shows a recruitment post on a Russian-language underground forum advertising a multifunctional infostealer with RAT capabilities explicitly designed to operate within antidetect browser environments, listing Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin among 21 compatible platforms capable of harvesting session cookies, authentication tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, API keys, and 2FA credentials.

Figure 6 – A recruitment post on a Russian-language underground forum lists 21 browsers including Kameleo, AdsPower, and MultiLogin as compatible platforms.

As seen in Figure 7, a threat actor on a Russian-language underground hacking forum explicitly introduces Kameleo as a component of Browser-in-the-Middle phishing kits targeting credentials across Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and financial platforms. In a Browser-in-the-Middle attack, the phishing server instructs the antidetect browser to create a new profile for the victim, assigned a residential proxy in their country and a clean device fingerprint. The victim’s credentials, entered on the phishing page, are passed in real time into the real login page of the target service through an automation framework. The target platform sees a login attempt from a consistent, locally coherent device with a residential IP address in the expected country, none of the signals that would trigger a security challenge or step-up authentication.

Figure 7 – A post on a Russian-language underground hacking forum introducing Kameleo as a component of Browser-in-the-Middle phishing kits targeting credentials across Google, Microsoft, Facebook, and financial platforms.

AdsPower

Chinese in origin and subsequently registered across multiple jurisdictions and localized into more than 20 languages, AdsPower applies fingerprint spoofing logic across more than 20 configurable parameters per profile and advertises a 99.2% ban avoidance rate. As seen in Figure 8, its proxy editor provides a built-in catalog of compatible third-party residential and rotating proxy providers, assignable directly within the profile creation interface. Figure 9 illustrates the granularity of fingerprint control available, with each profile’s WebRTC handling, time zone, geolocation, and language individually configurable to ensure the synthetic identity is consistent across every detectable signal.

Figure 8 – AdsPower’s proxy integration interface lists compatible third-party residential and rotating proxy providers available within the platform.

Figure 9 – AdsPower’s fingerprint editor displaying granular per-profile identity parameters including WebRTC, timezone and location derived from the assigned proxy IP.

The scale of AdsPower’s intended use is reflected in its pricing structure, with published tiers supporting up to 5,000 distinct profiles as seen in Figure 10, and enterprise arrangements available on request. As seen in Figure 11, its account editor supports platforms spanning social media, e-commerce, financial services, and professional networks including Facebook, Amazon, LinkedIn, X, PayPal, and Google.

Figure 10 – AdsPower’s pricing table reflects the intended operational scale, with enterprise tiers supporting more than 5,000 profiles available upon request.

Figure 11 – AdsPower’s account editor shows supported platforms available for bulk profile management, including Facebook, Amazon, LinkedIn, X, PayPal, and Google.

Scalability is further addressed through a built-in RPA engine and a dedicated Marketplace, as seen in Figure 12, offering pre-built templates for automated liking, commenting, direct messaging, follower scraping, and AI-assisted engagement across hundreds of profiles simultaneously. The multi-window synchronizer replicates identical actions across hundreds of profiles from a single input, while account warming automation builds synthetic activity histories over weeks to reduce platform suspicion before deployment.

Figure 12 – AdsPower’s RPA Marketplace lists pre-built automation templates for bulk account activity across major platforms, including automated liking, commenting, direct messaging, follower scraping, and AI-assisted engagement.

On the AI front, AdsPower advertises a dedicated Model Context Protocol server enabling direct integration with large language model workflows, creating a pipeline in which AI-generated content can be produced, injected into pre-warmed account profiles, and distributed across platforms in a fully automated sequence requiring no human involvement. A companion feature, the Cookie Robot, automates cookie warming on TikTok and Twitter/X accounts prior to operational use. The RPA Marketplace is the delivery mechanism for this pipeline, with ready-to-deploy workflows designed to operate in direct combination with AI-generated content, resulting in an end-to-end operation at a scale and speed previously associated only with state-sponsored actors.

As seen in Figure 13, AdsPower’s own published scraping guide explicitly acknowledges that scraping Facebook constitutes a violation of the platform’s terms of service and may result in legal action, before advising users that an antidetect browser can help bypass these limitations.

Figure 13 – AdsPower’s official scraping guide advises users that an antidetect browser can help bypass scraping limitations.

MultiLogin

MultiLogin operates as a fully featured antidetect browser platform, offering isolated browser profiles with unique device fingerprints covering canvas output, WebGL parameters, fonts, timezone, screen resolution, and user agent, with each profile maintaining separate cookies, local storage, and session data. The platform supports automation through Selenium, Playwright, and Puppeteer, enabling fully scripted, headless operation of multiple profiles simultaneously. MultiLogin has been referenced on Exploit, a Russian-language underground hacking forum, in a thread dedicated to antidetect browsers, indicating active discussion and adoption of the platform within criminal communities (see Figure 6).

MultiLogin extends its multi-account capability into the mobile layer through a phone farming infrastructure that replaces physical Android devices with cloud-hosted equivalents. Every cloud Android profile maintains its own persistent mobile device parameters, with proxies assigned per profile to control location and network identity. MultiLogin’s own documentation states that most account bans in phone farm environments occur due to multiple accounts sharing the same device signals, storage, or network patterns, and positions its product as the solution to this detection problem, an explicit acknowledgment that the platform is designed to defeat association detection at the mobile layer.

According to their website, virtual phone number provisioning through partner integrations enables SMS-based account verification without physical SIM cards or mobile devices. Each virtual number is paired with a mobile device fingerprint profile, enabling the rapid creation of large volumes of accounts that appear to originate from distinct mobile devices across different geographic locations.

MultiLogin maintains a dedicated web scraping solution page and publishes operational guides for scraping platforms including Facebook, LinkedIn, Amazon, and Twitter, with its built-in residential proxy infrastructure marketed as enabling scraping operations that bypass bot detection and IP-based rate limiting. Its stated use cases listed on its own website include ticket scalping automation, a practice explicitly illegal in multiple jurisdictions and prohibited by major ticketing platforms, with the platform’s infrastructure documented as tested daily against major ticketing services for compatibility. MultiLogin additionally lists AI Quick Actions Automation among its documented product capabilities, indicating a degree of AI integration into its operational workflow.

As seen in Figure 14, MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts cryptocurrency alongside credit card payments and regional systems including SberPay and YooMoney. Notably, YooMoney has been designated on the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals list since April 2022 under Executive Order 14024 as a Sberbank subsidiary, and SberPay operates as a product of Sberbank, itself under comprehensive OFAC blocking sanctions since February 2022. The acceptance of these payment methods, alongside cryptocurrency, enables anonymous and potentially sanctions-non-compliant transactions. MultiLogin offers 24/7 support through dedicated Telegram channels staffed by human representatives and is tested daily against more than 50 major social media platforms to ensure continued compatibility. Taken together, MultiLogin’s mobile infrastructure, AI automation layer, scraping capabilities, criminal community presence, and payment infrastructure make it one of the most operationally complete platforms in this category.

Figure 14 – MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts a variety of different payment services.

AI-Powered Campaign Infrastructure

The most consequential recent development is AI integration directly into the operational stack. AdsPower advertises a dedicated Model Context Protocol server enabling direct integration with large language model workflows, creating a pipeline in which AI-generated content can be produced, injected into pre-warmed account profiles, and distributed across platforms in a fully automated sequence requiring no human involvement. A companion feature, the Cookie Robot, automates cookie warming on TikTok and Twitter/X accounts prior to operational use, simulating browsing behavior to establish account credibility before the content distribution phase begins.

The RPA Marketplace mentioned in the previous section is the delivery mechanism for this pipeline. Available templates contain ready-to-deploy workflows maintained and updated by the vendor, designed to operate in direct combination with AI-generated content. This creates an end-to-end influence operation pipeline that requires no active operator presence once the campaign is initiated. The result is a single automated workflow that places coordinated influence operation capacity within reach of any sufficiently motivated actor, regardless of resources or technical expertise.

Web Scraping as Operational Intelligence

The web scraping capabilities documented across these platforms serve a function that extends well beyond data collection. Scraped data is the intelligence layer that makes the operation more precise. Several of the tools we reviewed maintain dedicated scraping solution pages describing capabilities including fingerprint rotation, CAPTCHA bypass, and headless browsing designed to extract data from platforms including LinkedIn, Amazon, Facebook, and Twitter while evading their anti-scraping defenses. As seen in Figure 13, the AdsPower published scraping guide explicitly acknowledges that scraping Facebook constitutes a violation of the platform’s terms of service and may result in legal action, before advising users that an antidetect browser can help bypass these limitations.

The combination of well-farmed personas and targeted scraping capabilities enables a precision influence operation at scale.

Workflow:

  1. An artificial account, warmed up over several weeks of simulated activity, accumulates sufficient credibility to be accepted into a closed group on a social media platform.
  2. Once inside, the platform’s scraping infrastructure extracts available information on every member, including names, profile data, religious affiliations, political interests, age, geographic markers, and engagement patterns.
  3. The harvested dataset becomes the targeting intelligence for a bulk coordinated campaign, allowing artificial personas to engage each member with content calibrated to their specific profile, amplify narratives that resonate with the group’s demonstrated interests, and simulate the kind of peer validation that drives genuine behavioral change.

A Sophisticated and Professionally Maintained Ecosystem

The commercial availability of these tools reflects a fundamental shift in the influence-operation threat landscape: what was once the domain of well-resourced state actors and advanced persistent threat groups is now accessible to any motivated individual with a credit card. These are all professionally maintained, customer-supported, multilingual software platforms with pricing pages, knowledge bases, release notes, and dedicated sales teams. The only barrier to running a large-scale coordinated inauthentic operation is not a user’s technical sophistication but the need to pay a subscription fee.

The language coverage and market reach of these tools reflects the scale of their intended user base. AdsPower is available in 20 languages. MultiLogin supports English, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, and Portuguese, and is tested daily against more than 50 platforms. Kameleo maintains a public blog catalog of dedicated technical guides on bypassing Cloudflare bot detection, defeating DataDome, and solving Cloudflare Turnstile challenges, which are all security systems deployed specifically to identify and block automated or inauthentic browser sessions.

The customer support infrastructure surrounding these tools mirrors that of legitimate enterprise software, with MultiLogin offering 24/7 support through dedicated Telegram channels staffed by human representatives. As seen in Figure 14, MultiLogin’s payment infrastructure accepts cryptocurrency alongside credit card payments and regional systems including SberPay and YooMoney, both Russian payment services.

As seen in Figure 15, independent threat actors have developed and are actively selling purpose-built antidetect solutions on underground forums, complete with feature documentation, technical support, and monthly subscription pricing. This particular tool targets Android devices specifically, offering automated geolocation spoofing, device ID replacement, Wi-Fi environment manipulation, and Play Integrity bypass at 100 USD per month, reflecting the breadth of threat actor demand across different device categories and operational requirements.

As seen in Figure 16, the downstream commercial activity built on this infrastructure extends to farmed platform accounts advertised for sale on underground forums alongside explicit instructions to access them using antidetect browsers. Cryptocurrency is the default payment method. These posts confirm a mature commercial underground market in which these antidetect tools function as the operational backbone of a broader fraud and influence ecosystem.

Figure 15 – An antidetect tool designed for Android devices advertised on an underground forum, offers automated geolocation spoofing, device ID replacement, and Play Integrity bypass at 100 USD per month.

Figure 16 – Farmed Google Ads accounts advertised for sale on an underground forum.

Conclusion

The antidetect browser ecosystem represents a sophisticated, commercially mature, and increasingly AI-driven infrastructure that has fundamentally lowered the barrier to running scam and fraud operations, as well as coordinated inauthentic operations at scale. These commercially maintained tools are available in dozens of languages, backed by customer support teams, tested daily against the world’s largest social media platforms, and are now integrated with LLM pipelines that remove the human operator from the execution layer. The coupling of identity spoofing infrastructure, automated content distribution, and AI-assisted persona management represents a threat surface that platform detection systems may struggle to address, particularly in the context of elections taking place across multiple countries.

The infrastructure we documented is commercially available today. Its capabilities are not constrained by technical sophistication, national resources, or operational scale. The question is no longer whether these tools are being actively used for fraud, account takeover, and coordinated manipulation, but whether the detection, enforcement, and awareness frameworks across every layer of the ecosystem are prepared to counter them.

Recommendations

Security and threat intelligence teams:

  • The detection priority should shift from the account and behavioral layer, where these tools are already designed to appear invisible, to the network and infrastructure layer.
  • Indicators include residential proxy infrastructure operating at scale, WebRTC suppression patterns, anomalous cookie injection sequences, and known antidetect browser user agent strings in web traffic logs.
  • Account warming patterns, simulated by these tools over several weeks, may be indistinguishable from legitimate organic behavior without cross-referencing device fingerprint consistency over time.

Social media platforms:

  • Antidetectbrowser infrastructure should be treated as a first-class priority.
  • The capabilities operate below existing detection thresholds, and infrastructure-layer signals may be the only reliable detection surface available.
  • Platforms should consider actively acquiring and reverse engineering antidetect tools to map their proxy patterns, fingerprint rotation behaviors, and detection bypass mechanisms, and use those findings to recalibrate banning logic specifically against these tools’ TTPs.

CISOs and companies:

  • The risk posed by antidetect browser infrastructure extends well beyond influence operations.
  • Silent account takeover using cookie injection workflows can bypass multi-factor authentication without generating a login event.
  • Organizations are advised to review whether their session monitoring infrastructure can detect pre-authenticated session anomalies, and to incorporate antidetect-specific attack scenarios into red team exercises and threat models.
  • Threat actors can leverage antidetect browsers to replicate victim device fingerprints and geolocation to execute unauthorized transactions without triggering behavioral anomaly detection.
  • Fraud detection systems that rely on device consistency and session continuity signals should be specifically reviewed for resilience against fingerprint spoofing and session injection at the identity infrastructure layer.

The post The Risk of AI-Powered Antidetect Browsers in Online Fraud and Influence Operations appeared first on Check Point Research.

[…]

According to Cellebrite, AU:

  • is a “next-generation AFU vector that is more resilient to Apple’s OS changes”

item.content:encoded:
Justin.sh is reporting on a confidential Cellebrite document that has been leaked to him:

Cellebrite calls it Advanced Unlocks (AU from here on), not to be confused with the “advanced unlocking services” they’ve marketed for years. A press release from earlier this year confirms AU is a new product for 2026.

[…]

According to Cellebrite, AU:

  • is a “next-generation AFU vector that is more resilient to Apple’s OS changes”
  • works with Stolen Device Protection enabled, which tightens USB restrictions
  • is enabled by a dedicated appliance with a stated range (!) of about 8 meters.

AU = Advanced Unlocks, Cellebrite’s term. AFU = after first unlock.
